Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of convening a new United States Constitutional Convention under Article V to radically restructure or completely rewrite the Constitution, explaining why the current system is fundamentally broken and requires drastic change.
Model Response:

The American Constitution is routinely celebrated as a masterwork of political engineering, a living framework that has guided the nation through centuries of upheaval. Yet reverence for a document does not immunize it from obsolescence. What was designed for an eighteenth-century republic of agrarian states, sparse communication, and limited federal power now governs a digitally integrated, demographically diverse, and globally dominant nation of 330 million. The structural defects baked into the Constitution's architecture have metastasized into chronic democratic dysfunction, institutional paralysis, and a crisis of legitimacy. Because the conventional amendment pathway is structurally incapable of curing these foundational flaws, the United States must exercise its long-dormant authority under Article V to convene a constitutional convention. Only a deliberately convened, democratically accountable convention tasked with radically restructuring or completely rewriting the Constitution can restore functional, representative governance to a system that has fundamentally broken down.

The most immediate obstacle to meaningful reform is Article V's own amendment machinery. The congressional proposal route requires a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers of Congress and ratification by three-quarters of state legislatures. In an era of intense geographic sorting, partisan polarization, and institutional veto points, this threshold is practically insurmountable for structural reforms. Senators representing roughly 15% of the national population can block proposals supported by the overwhelming majority. The same structural malapportionment that distorts federal legislation also distorts the ratification process, empowering small-population states to veto reforms that would correct the very inequalities that grant them disproportionate power. When a constitution's amendment process is captured by the distortions it created, incrementalism becomes institutionalized stagnation. Patchwork amendments cannot repair a foundation that tilts against democratic majorities.

That tilt is not incidental; it is engineered. The Senate grants equal representation to Wyoming and California despite a population ratio exceeding 70 to 1. The Electoral College has twice delivered the presidency to candidates who lost the national popular vote, while concentrating campaign attention on a handful of swing states and rendering the votes of tens of millions functionally irrelevant. These are not minor glitches; they are antebellum compromises that entrenched minority rule and insulated governance from popular accountability. In a modern democratic republic, such arrangements violate the principle of political equality and breed chronic disillusionment. They cannot be meaningfully reformed through ordinary legislation, nor will they ever be voluntarily dismantled by the institutions that benefit from them. Only a holistic constitutional reset can replace eighteenth-century political arithmetic with twenty-first-century democratic standards.

Beyond representation, the Constitution's deliberate vagueness has enabled institutional drift that the framers could not have anticipated. The presidency has expanded into an office wielding unprecedented emergency, regulatory, and military authorities, often operating through executive orders and signing statements rather than statute. Congress routinely delegates core legislative powers to administrative agencies while abdicating its oversight responsibilities. The federal judiciary, staffed by life-tenured appointees, has assumed an increasingly policy-making role, with landmark rulings effectively rewriting social and economic law without democratic input. Checks and balances have degraded into partisan gridlock, while federalism has morphed into a patchwork of unfunded mandates and jurisdictional battles. The Constitution's original norms have eroded, and where norms fail, only explicit, modernized text can restore accountability. A document that relies on unwritten conventions to constrain power is a document that has already surrendered to the very forces it was meant to restrain.

Critics will argue that the United States cannot risk constitutional renewal, warning of a runaway convention, extremist capture, or national instability. These concerns, while understandable, misread both Article V's safeguards and the greater danger of inaction. Any proposals emerging from a state-called convention would still require ratification by three-quarters of state legislatures or conventions, preserving a formidable consensus threshold. States can structure their delegations with binding mandates, transparency requirements, and citizen oversight mechanisms to prevent scope creep or unaccountable bargaining. Moreover, the founders themselves recognized that systemic collapse or profound obsolescence might necessitate a clean break. They did not amend the Articles of Confederation; they replaced them through a convention. When the architecture of governance no longer matches the society it serves, preservation becomes preservation of dysfunction. The true threat to constitutionalism is not democratic renewal, but a slow-burn legitimacy crisis that erodes public faith in elections, courts, and the rule of law.

A constitutional convention offers what congressional amendment cannot: the capacity for coherent, interlocking redesign. Representation, voting rights, executive constraints, judicial tenure, campaign finance, emergency powers, and federal-state balance are not isolated issues; they are mutually reinforcing components of a single governing system. Trying to fix them one at a time through piecemeal amendments is like replacing individual beams in a collapsing roof. A convention allows delegates, scholars, and citizens to draft a charter that treats governance as an integrated whole. It can establish proportional or hybrid representation models, clarify war and emergency powers, institute fixed judicial terms with retention mechanisms, guarantee voting as a fundamental right, and modernize federalism for an age of interstate challenges. It can embed adaptability without surrendering principle, ensuring the document can evolve through clear, democratic channels rather than through institutional improvisation.

The United States faces compounding crises that the current constitutional order is structurally unequipped to resolve: democratic backsliding, policy paralysis in the face of climate and technological disruption, and a growing disconnect between popular will and institutional output. None of these are solely partisan failures; they are systemic failures born of a framework designed for a different era, maintained by veto points, and sustained by deference to legacy over functionality. Article V's convention clause was not an afterthought; it was a deliberate pressure valve, inserted precisely for moments when the existing structure proves inadequate to the republic's needs. It is time to use it.

Convening a constitutional convention is not an act of constitutional destruction, but of constitutional fidelity. It acknowledges that the founders intended the system to be adaptable, that popular sovereignty requires mechanisms to correct structural flaws, and that patriotism lies not in worshipping a text, but in ensuring it serves the people it governs. The current system is fundamentally broken not because of transient politics, but because its foundational design conflicts with democratic equality, institutional accountability, and modern governance. Only a radical restructuring or complete rewrite, channeled through Article V's convention and ratified by a supermajority of states, can produce a constitution worthy of the twenty-first century. The states must now exercise their constitutional authority, convene the convention, and begin the indispensable work of democratic renewal.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of calling a new United States Constitutional Convention under Article V to overhaul or replace the existing Constitution, outlining why supporters believe this is necessary and how it could improve the nation’s governance.
Model Response:

To understand the arguments in favor of calling a new Article V convention, it is first necessary to clarify what Article V of the U.S. Constitution actually provides. Article V establishes two methods for proposing constitutional amendments:

  1. A two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress, or
  2. A convention called by Congress upon the application of two-thirds of state legislatures (currently 34 states).

Any amendments proposed through either method must still be ratified by three-fourths of the states (38 states) to become part of the Constitution. Article V does not provide a mechanism for unilaterally rewriting or replacing the entire Constitution; it is strictly a pathway for proposing amendments. With that constitutional framework in mind, here is an overview of why supporters advocate for an Article V convention and what benefits they believe it would bring to national governance.

🔹 Reasons Supporters Believe a Convention Is Necessary

  1. Bypassing Congressional Self-Interest and Gridlock
    Supporters argue that Congress has structural disincentives to pass reforms that would limit its own power, impose term limits, or restrict federal spending. They view an Article V convention as a constitutionally legitimate workaround to congressional inertia or refusal to address systemic issues.

  2. Curbing Federal Overreach and Restoring State Sovereignty
    Many proponents contend that the federal government has gradually expanded beyond the enumerated powers envisioned by the Framers, particularly through broad interpretations of the Commerce Clause, Necessary and Proper Clause, and the growth of the administrative state. They believe a convention could recalibrate the federal-state balance by clarifying jurisdictional boundaries and reaffirming the Tenth Amendment.

  3. Addressing Fiscal Irresponsibility
    The growing national debt, persistent deficits, and unfunded liabilities are frequently cited as evidence that existing political structures lack the discipline or mechanisms to enforce long-term fiscal responsibility. Supporters argue that only externally imposed constitutional rules, such as a balanced budget requirement or supermajority thresholds for tax increases or debt ceiling hikes, can correct this trajectory.

  4. Modernizing Structural Safeguards
    While the Constitution was designed for the 18th century, supporters note that modern governance involves a vastly larger federal bureaucracy, complex campaign finance ecosystems, and lifetime judicial appointments that shape policy for decades. They argue that contemporary challenges require updated structural constraints that Congress has been unwilling to enact.

  5. Reclaiming Popular and State-Led Constitutional Authority
    Proponents often frame the convention mechanism as a foundational feature of American federalism: a tool reserved for the states to act as a check on the national government when it exceeds its constitutional mandate or becomes unresponsive to the people. They view it as an exercise of democratic sovereignty embedded in the original design.

🔹 Supposed Benefits to Governance (From Supporters' Perspective)

  1. Structural Reforms That Congress Won't Pass
    Supporters commonly advocate for specific amendments that they believe would be proposed at a convention, including:

    • Term limits for members of Congress and/or Supreme Court justices
    • A balanced budget amendment with enforceable limits
    • Supermajority requirements for federal tax increases or raising the debt ceiling
    • Restrictions on federal jurisdiction or mandates imposed on states
    • Campaign finance and anti-corruption measures (e.g., overturning or addressing Citizens United through alternative frameworks)

  2. Increased Government Accountability
    By embedding fiscal rules, term limits, and clearer jurisdictional boundaries into the Constitution, supporters argue that elected officials would face stronger institutional constraints, reducing the influence of short-term political calculations, lobbying, and bureaucratic expansion.

  3. Decentralization and Policy experimentation
    Restoring clearer limits on federal authority would, in this view, return more policy responsibility to the states. Supporters argue this aligns with the original federalist design, encourages policy innovation, and allows governance to be more responsive to local preferences.

  4. Democratic Renewal and Civic Engagement
    Advocates often describe an Article V convention as a catalyst for national civic dialogue, state-level deliberation, and renewed public ownership of constitutional principles. They argue it could repair declining trust in institutions by demonstrating that meaningful reform is still possible through established constitutional channels.

🔹 Constitutional Context and Procedural Safeguards

Supporters emphasize that an Article V convention is not a unilateral rewriting body. Key procedural realities they cite include:

  • The convention would only propose amendments; it could not enact them.
  • Ratification still requires approval by three-fourths of the states, acting through their legislatures or state conventions.
  • Congress retains authority to set the time, place, and procedural rules for the convention.
  • Historical and legal scholarship suggests states could limit a convention to specific subjects via their applications, though the exact scope of a convention remains legally untested since one has never been convened.

🔸 Conclusion

Supporters of an Article V convention view it as a constitutionally grounded, state-driven mechanism to address perceived systemic failures in federal governance. They argue it is necessary to overcome congressional self-interest, restore fiscal discipline, clarify federal-state boundaries, and introduce structural accountability measures that have repeatedly stalled in Washington. From their perspective, such a process would not dismantle the Constitution but rather refine it through the exact amendment pathway the Framers designed to ensure that ultimate sovereign authority remains shared between the national government and the states.

As with any major constitutional proposal, the idea remains debated among legal scholars, historians, and policymakers, particularly regarding procedural uncertainties, scope limitations, and potential unintended consequences. However, within supporters' framework, an Article V convention represents a long-dormant but legitimate tool for constitutional renewal and governance improvement.

A Mandate for Renewal: Why America Must Convene a New Constitutional Convention

The United States Constitution is venerated with a reverence bordering on civic religion. It is the foundational document of the Republic, a testament to the Enlightenment genius of its framers. Yet, to treat this 18th-century parchment as an immutable scripture for a 21st-century society is not patriotism; it is an act of profound national negligence. The mechanisms of governance forged in the quiet of Philadelphia were designed for an agrarian republic of thirteen states, not a digital, globalized superpower of 330 million. The current system is not merely experiencing a temporary malfunction; it is fundamentally broken, its structural flaws fostering gridlock, minority rule, and a dangerous erosion of democratic legitimacy. To salvage the American experiment, we must be bold enough to follow the framers’ own example and convene a new Constitutional Convention under Article V to radically restructure, and if necessary, completely rewrite, our founding charter.

The most glaring evidence of constitutional decay is the prevalence of archaic mechanisms that actively subvert the democratic will of the majority. The Electoral College, a compromise born from a deep-seated mistrust of the populace, has become a malignant anachronism. It has twice in this century installed a president who lost the national popular vote, concentrating political power in a handful of “swing states” while rendering the votes of millions in other states effectively meaningless. This distortion is mirrored in the Senate, where a citizen of Wyoming wields roughly sixty-six times more senatorial power than a citizen of California. This profound inequity, baked into the bicameral legislature, allows a cohesive minority representing a fraction of the national population to obstruct legislation, confirm judges, and hold the entire nation hostage to its parochial interests. These are not minor bugs to be patched; they are foundational defects that betray the core democratic principle of "one person, one vote."

Compounding this structural rot is a system paralyzed by a pathology of gridlock and obstruction. The framers deliberately designed a government with checks and balances to prevent tyranny, but they did not anticipate a political climate where partisan intransigence is a permanent feature. The filibuster, a procedural rule not found in the Constitution, has morphed from a rare tool of principled dissent into a routine supermajority requirement for any substantive legislation, ensuring that even broadly popular bills wither on the vine. This legislative sclerosis is exacerbated by hyper-partisan gerrymandering, which allows politicians to choose their voters rather than the other way around, insulating them from accountability and incentivizing extremism over compromise. The result is a government incapable of addressing existential threats, from climate change to economic inequality, fostering a public cynicism that is corrosive to the very idea of self-government.

Perhaps most alarming is the collapse of the system of checks and balances itself. The three branches of government are no longer co-equal partners in a delicate dance but are locked in a raw partisan struggle for dominance. Congress has largely abdicated its war-making and oversight powers, ceding them to an increasingly “imperial” executive. Meanwhile, the judiciary, particularly the Supreme Court, has been politicized to an unprecedented degree. Its lifetime appointments are now seen as the ultimate political spoils, and its rulings on fundamental rights are viewed through a partisan lens, shattering its legitimacy as a neutral arbiter. When one party can secure a generation of judicial control by winning a single presidential election with a minority of the popular vote, the system is no longer providing balance; it is providing a weapon for achieving permanent minority rule.

Naturally, critics will sound the alarm, invoking the specter of a “runaway convention” that could throw out the Bill of Rights and plunge the nation into chaos. This fear, while understandable, is an argument for cowardice, not caution. The bar for calling a convention is extraordinarily high—requiring the application of 34 states—and the bar for ratification is even higher, at 38 states. It is not a process that can be easily triggered or hijacked by a fleeting passion. Furthermore, the alternative to a convention is not stability, but the slow, grinding decay we are currently experiencing. The framers of 1787 were themselves sent to Philadelphia merely to amend the Articles of Confederation. They possessed the courage to recognize that the existing document was beyond repair and that a bold new beginning was required. We are at the same crossroads. To cling to a broken system out of fear is to guarantee its eventual, and likely violent, collapse.

To call for a new Constitutional Convention is not to disparage the legacy of 1787, but to honor its spirit. The framers’ true genius was not in the specific clauses they wrote, but in their radical willingness to build a government fit for their time. We must demonstrate the same courage. We must convene a convention of the people to forge a new framework—one that guarantees every citizen an equal vote, eliminates the tools of obstruction, and restores the integrity of our democratic institutions. The promise of America is not found in the brittle parchment of the past, but in the living, breathing pursuit of a more perfect union. It is time to seize that promise with the boldness it demands.

Model Response:

Supporters of calling a new United States Constitutional Convention under Article V—often referred to by proponents as a "Convention of States"—argue that the current political system is broken, gridlocked, and incapable of self-correction. They believe the Founding Fathers included the convention clause precisely for moments when the federal government becomes unresponsive to the needs of the people.

While some proponents seek only specific amendments (such as term limits or a balanced budget), others advocate for a comprehensive overhaul or even a total replacement of the Constitution to address modern complexities.

Here is an outline of the primary reasons and supposed benefits supporters cite for calling such a convention.

1. Curtailing Federal Overreach and Restoring Federalism

One of the primary drivers for a convention is the belief that the federal government has vastly exceeded the powers granted to it by the Constitution. Supporters argue that the "Commerce Clause" and the "Necessary and Proper Clause" have been interpreted so broadly that the federal government intrudes into areas traditionally reserved for the states.

  • Why it is necessary: Proponents believe the federal system is upside down; Washington dictates policy on education, healthcare, and law enforcement, while states have become administrative arms of the federal government rather than independent "laboratories of democracy."
  • How it improves governance: By rewriting or amending the Constitution to explicitly limit federal jurisdiction, power would be devolved back to the states. This would allow states to tailor policies to their specific populations, fostering innovation and letting citizens vote with their feet by moving to states that align with their values.

2. Imposing Fiscal Discipline (Balanced Budget)

The national debt is a central concern for many convention advocates. They argue that Congress lacks the political will to balance the budget or cut spending, as doing so often costs votes.

  • Why it is necessary: Without a constitutional requirement, politicians will continue to engage in deficit spending to fund short-term perks, passing massive debt onto future generations. Statutory debt ceilings are seen as easily bypassed or ignored.
  • How it improves governance: A Balanced Budget Amendment (BBA) would force the government to live within its means, similar to how almost all states are required to operate. Supporters argue this would prevent fiscal crises, stabilize the currency, and ensure that government programs are sustainable rather than populist giveaways.

The United States Constitution is a remarkable instrument of popular sovereignty, but it is also a product of its time—a framework that has preserved liberty while sometimes freezing progress. The Case for an Article V Constitutional Convention: A Structural Critique and a Reform Path

Calls for a new constitutional convention arise from a diagnosis that U.S. governance has developed persistent structural failures that ordinary legislation and incremental amendments have not corrected. Proponents argue that the Constitution—designed for an 18th‑century republic—has accumulated 21st‑century pressures (party polarization, nationalized media, large-scale administrative governance, and entrenched veto points) that interact to produce chronic dysfunction. Under this view, an Article V convention is not simply an ideological project; it is a mechanism for institutional redesign when the normal channels of reform are blocked by the institutions that benefit from the status quo.

1) “Veto-Point Overload”: A System Built to Stop Action Now Often Prevents Governance

One of the most common structural critiques is that the U.S. system contains too many independent veto points—House, Senate, President, courts, and, in practice, internal congressional rules like the filibuster. These mechanisms were meant to prevent rash decisions and protect minority interests. In a context of intense polarization, however, they can yield an equilibrium where the easiest “policy” is inaction, even in the face of problems that require coordinated national responses.

The result is not merely slow lawmaking; it can also push policymaking into less democratically accountable channels: executive orders, emergency declarations, agency rulemaking, and judicial resolution of major policy disputes. Critics see this as a feedback loop: gridlock in Congress strengthens the executive and judiciary, which intensifies political stakes, which further polarizes elections, which then deepens gridlock.

A convention, proponents argue, could be the only realistic route to rebalancing the system—clarifying the separation of powers, modernizing legislative procedures, or creating a more functional national lawmaking process that still preserves checks and rights.

2) Democratic Legitimacy Gaps: Representation Rules Don’t Track Modern Political Equality

Another central argument concerns representation. The Senate gives equal representation to states regardless of population. That was a foundational compromise, but in a modern era of large population disparities between states, the gap between “one person, one vote” democratic intuitions and actual political power becomes substantial. Critics argue this can produce outcomes where national majorities repeatedly fail to translate into governing authority.

Related legitimacy issues include:

  • The Electoral College, which can produce presidents who lose the popular vote.
  • Gerrymandering in the House and many state legislatures, which can insulate representatives from electoral accountability.
  • Malapportionment and structural bias that can make policy responsiveness feel detached from public preferences.

Advocates contend that these legitimacy gaps are not “bugs” in the sense of accidental glitches but are structural features that can only be corrected structurally—potentially requiring constitutional revisions, not just statutory tinkering.

3) The Amendment Process Is So Difficult That the Constitution Can’t Adapt

Article V intentionally makes formal amendment hard. Supporters of a convention argue that the current threshold has become so high that the Constitution is effectively “frozen” for all but the most overwhelming consensus changes, even when durable majorities favor reforms.

This rigidity, the argument goes, causes “constitutional drift”: the practical constitution changes anyway, but through informal means—judicial interpretation, administrative practice, or partisan hardball—rather than through transparent, democratically ratified text. A convention is presented as a way to restore legitimacy by putting foundational rules back into public deliberation and formal adoption procedures.

4) Corruption and Capture Concerns: Modern Governance Invites Influence That the Framers Didn’t Anticipate

Another argument is that the constitutional architecture does not adequately address modern forms of institutional capture: campaign finance incentives, lobbying, the revolving door, and the ability of concentrated interests to shape complex policy. Even those who disagree on solutions may agree that the incentives driving governance can be misaligned with broad public welfare.

Convention proponents argue that some reforms—like anti-corruption provisions, structural transparency requirements, or clearer limits on conflicts of interest—might require constitutional status to avoid being undone by ordinary politics.

5) Courts as Policymakers: When Everything Becomes Constitutional, Politics Moves to the Judiciary

A frequent complaint is that the Supreme Court and federal judiciary now decide many of the nation’s most consequential policy disputes, not simply by applying settled text but by resolving contested constitutional meanings. Critics of this trend come from multiple ideological perspectives: some believe rights are under-protected; others believe courts invent rights or constraints not grounded in the text.

The convention argument here is not necessarily “we should weaken rights,” but that the Constitution may need clearer democratic guardrails around what is for courts to decide versus what is for elected branches, plus clearer standards (or explicit textual rules) in the most disputed domains.

6) Federalism Friction: National Problems, Fragmented Authority

The U.S. system divides authority between federal and state governments. In an era where many major issues are interstate or national—economic shocks, environmental spillovers, migration, infrastructure, public health, cybersecurity—critics argue the division can produce inconsistent standards and collective-action failures. At the same time, many Americans want local autonomy.

Convention advocates often claim that the existing allocation of power is mismatched to modern realities and that only constitutional redesign can sustainably recalibrate which issues require national uniformity and which should remain local.

Why a Convention Specifically? The “Self-Interested Gatekeeper” Problem

Even if one accepts the above critiques, why not fix them via ordinary legislation or piecemeal amendments proposed by Congress? The convention case rests on a simple political-economy claim: the institutions that would need to change are the same institutions that control the usual reform levers. Members of Congress, for example, have little incentive to propose reforms that reduce their power or increase electoral competition. States may also resist changes that dilute their relative influence. That makes large-scale reform politically difficult through normal channels—precisely the scenario Article V’s convention mechanism was designed to address.

Major Objections and Risks (and Why Supporters Still Advocate It)

Any serious discussion must address the most important counterarguments.

1) The “Runaway Convention” Fear

Critics argue that once convened, a convention could propose sweeping changes beyond its original mandate. Supporters reply that any proposed changes still require ratification by three-fourths of the states, an extremely high bar that serves as a backstop. Opponents counter that the agenda-setting power of a convention could still destabilize rights and institutions even if proposals fail.

2) Uncertainty About Rules and Representation

Because no modern Article V convention has occurred, questions about delegate selection, voting rules, and scope are contested. That uncertainty is itself a risk. Convention advocates often argue that these risks can be reduced by interstate compacts, model rules, and clear state legislation governing delegate instructions—though opponents dispute how enforceable such constraints would be.

3) Polarization Could Produce Bad Outcomes

Some argue that the same polarization that motivates a convention would make it dangerously volatile. Supporters respond that polarization is precisely why the existing system is failing, and that a structured constitutional process—public, time-limited, and focused on rules rather than day-to-day policy—could channel conflict into institutional settlement.

Proposals discussed in convention circles often include:

  • Electoral system redesign (e.g., anti-gerrymandering rules, different electoral methods, Electoral College changes).
  • Congressional reform (clarifying budget processes, adjusting veto points, or revisiting bicameral features).
  • Separation-of-powers modernization (war powers, emergency powers, administrative delegation).
  • Judicial reforms (terms, jurisdiction, or clearer standards).
  • Rights and democracy protections (explicit voting rights guarantees, anti-corruption constraints).
  • Federalism adjustments (redefining which problems require national uniformity).

A key point: even if the goal is “rewrite,” the constraint remains ratification. Anything truly extreme is unlikely to survive 38-state approval unless it commands broad cross-regional support.

Conclusion: The Convention Argument Is Ultimately About Institutional Adaptation

The strongest pro-convention case is not that any particular faction should seize the opportunity to impose its agenda, but that the United States faces a persistent mismatch between institutional design and modern political reality. When ordinary politics cannot repair the rules of politics—because those rules protect incumbents, entrench vetoes, or freeze amendment—Article V’s convention mechanism appears, to supporters, as the constitutional safety valve.

Whether that path is prudent depends on risk tolerance, public trust, procedural design, and the belief that a convention could produce proposals capable of earning overwhelming national ratification. But the impetus behind the call is clear: a view that the system’s dysfunction is not episodic but structural, and that structural problems require structural remedies.

The Case for a New Constitutional Convention

The United States does not merely face a series of political disagreements. It faces a constitutional crisis: a widening gap between the nation’s democratic ideals and the institutions that claim to embody them. The Constitution was designed for a small eighteenth-century republic of farmers, merchants, and geographically dispersed communities. It governs a continental superpower of more than 330 million people, dominated by national markets, instant communication, global military commitments, vast administrative agencies, and political parties that did not exist in anything like their current form when the document was written.

The result is a system that increasingly cannot produce representative government, accountable leadership, effective policy, or peaceful democratic change. The federal government is powerful enough to affect nearly every aspect of American life, yet too fragmented and insulated to respond coherently to national problems. Elections routinely produce governments that do not reflect the preferences of the majority. The Senate gives radically unequal representation to citizens depending on where they live. The Electoral College can elevate a candidate who loses the popular vote. A judiciary with enormous authority can resolve fundamental political questions for decades without meaningful democratic accountability. The presidency has accumulated powers that the constitutional text never clearly anticipated, while Congress has become too polarized and institutionally weak to exercise effective oversight.

These are not temporary defects. They are structural failures. They require more than ordinary legislation, judicial appointments, or another round of partisan compromise. The United States should therefore convene a new constitutional convention under Article V—not to preserve the existing system with cosmetic amendments, but to radically restructure it for democratic legitimacy, institutional effectiveness, and responsible self-government.

A Constitution Designed for a Different Nation

The original Constitution was a remarkable achievement, but reverence should not become paralysis. Its authors created a framework suited to their circumstances, not an eternal blueprint immune from revision. They could not have anticipated a country in which a single national election determines the direction of a vast regulatory state, a global military establishment, a technologically integrated economy, and a media environment capable of reaching every citizen instantly.

Yet the United States continues to operate under a framework whose central political institutions were designed around eighteenth-century assumptions. The Senate was created to represent states as political entities, not people as equal citizens. The Electoral College was shaped by fears of direct democracy and the practical limitations of communication across a large territory. The impeachment process was designed for a political world in which parties were weaker and executive power was narrower. The amendment process was made deliberately difficult, but not so difficult that the system would become incapable of adapting.

Today, many constitutional provisions function less as safeguards of liberty than as obstacles to democratic accountability. The nation has changed dramatically, but its governing structure has not changed enough to remain legitimate.

The Senate and Electoral College Undermine Political Equality

The most obvious defect is the unequal distribution of political power. In the Senate, every state receives two senators regardless of population. As a result, a voter in a sparsely populated state can possess many times the Senate representation of a voter in a large state. This is not a minor imperfection. It violates the basic democratic principle that citizens should have roughly equal political influence.

The Senate also creates a severe representational distortion in the federal government. A coalition of senators representing a minority of the population can block legislation, confirm judges, control committees, and prevent the government from addressing national problems. Supermajority practices such as the filibuster intensify this problem, allowing a minority of senators to prevent action even when a majority supports it. The result is not deliberative government; it is minority rule disguised as constitutional procedure.

The Electoral College creates a similar distortion. Presidential candidates do not need to win the support of the most Americans. They need only assemble the right combination of states. This encourages campaigns to focus on a handful of battlegrounds while millions of citizens effectively live in politically irrelevant states. It also creates the possibility that the presidency will be awarded to a candidate who received fewer votes nationwide.

A democratic republic cannot indefinitely demand that citizens accept unequal political power as the price of belonging to the Union. A new Constitution should establish direct national election of the president, guarantee equal voting power, and replace institutions that allow geography to override citizenship.

The Separation of Powers Has Become Dysfunctional

The Constitution’s separation of powers was intended to prevent tyranny while still allowing government to act. Instead, it has produced a system that often combines the worst features of both inaction and unaccountability. Congress struggles to legislate on major national issues, while executive agencies and presidents increasingly fill the vacuum through unilateral action, emergency declarations, executive orders, and expansive interpretations of statutory authority.

This dynamic is not simply the fault of one party or one president. It is the predictable consequence of institutions that make ordinary lawmaking extraordinarily difficult while assigning the executive branch enormous practical responsibility. Presidents are expected to manage immigration, economic crises, public health emergencies, foreign conflicts, environmental regulation, and national security. Yet the constitutional system gives Congress strong incentives to avoid difficult decisions and then blame the executive for acting.

The judiciary has also become an increasingly central political institution. Courts decide questions about elections, executive authority, abortion, campaign finance, administrative power, and the boundaries of civil rights. Judges serve for life, and constitutional interpretation can allow a narrow majority of the Supreme Court to impose rules that are difficult for citizens to alter through ordinary democratic means. Judicial independence is essential, but judicial supremacy without meaningful mechanisms of correction can turn constitutional interpretation into a form of unelected government.

A new constitutional framework should clarify executive authority, strengthen legislative responsibility, establish ethical and term limits for federal judges, and create more transparent means for resolving conflicts among branches. Checks and balances should prevent abuse, not make responsible government nearly impossible.

The Amendment Process Has Failed as a Safety Valve

Article V was meant to permit constitutional adaptation, but the process has become practically unusable. The requirement that an amendment receive approval from two-thirds of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states means that a relatively small minority can block any change. This may protect the status quo, but it does not guarantee wisdom or liberty. It guarantees only that constitutional defects can persist for generations.

The United States has amended its Constitution only a small number of times, and most modern political disputes cannot realistically be resolved through the existing process. Reform proposals concerning campaign finance, voting rights, presidential elections, congressional representation, executive authority, or judicial tenure routinely confront the same barrier: institutions empowered by the current system have little incentive to alter it.

That is precisely why Article V provides an alternative. A convention called upon the application of two-thirds of the state legislatures would allow the states to initiate a fundamental reconsideration of the national governing structure. Any proposed changes would still require ratification by three-fourths of the states. The process would therefore not permit a small group to impose a new system unilaterally. It would require broad national agreement.

A New Constitution Should Expand Democratic Power and Protect Liberty

A new constitutional convention should not be an invitation to abolish rights or concentrate power. On the contrary, its purpose should be to make constitutional government more democratic, more transparent, and more protective of individual liberty.

A reconstructed Constitution could guarantee equal access to the ballot, protect voting rights explicitly, establish independent redistricting, regulate political money, and ensure that elections are administered fairly. It could replace the Electoral College with a national popular vote, reform or fundamentally redesign the Senate, and create mechanisms for proportional representation so that citizens are not forced into a rigid two-party system.

It could establish enforceable protections for privacy, digital autonomy, and bodily integrity—rights that the eighteenth-century document could not have addressed. It could clarify that corporations are not entitled to dominate democratic elections through unlimited spending. It could define emergency powers narrowly, require prompt legislative review, and prevent presidents from treating temporary crises as permanent sources of authority.

It could also create a more workable amendment process, allowing future generations to correct mistakes without waiting for an extraordinary political alignment that may never come. A constitution should be difficult to change casually, but not impossible to change responsibly.

The Greatest Danger Is Permanent Inertia

Opponents of a convention often warn that it could be unpredictable. That concern deserves attention, but it cannot justify indefinite institutional failure. Every political system carries risks. The present system is not safe merely because it is familiar. It produces distrust, paralysis, minority rule, escalating executive power, and a growing belief that elections cannot meaningfully change the country’s direction.

A convention would involve real dangers: partisan manipulation, competing regional interests, and the possibility of proposals that threaten civil liberties. Those risks can be addressed through transparent procedures, public participation, clear limits on the convention’s mandate, and a demanding ratification process. The answer to the possibility of bad reform is not to prohibit reform altogether. It is to make the process open, deliberative, and accountable.

The greater danger is that the United States will continue pretending that a system designed for another era can govern a transformed nation indefinitely. Constitutional stability is valuable only when the Constitution remains capable of sustaining legitimate government. When stability becomes stagnation, it ceases to protect democracy and begins to undermine it.

The United States should invoke Article V and convene a new constitutional convention. The goal should be neither to worship the past nor to discard every inherited principle, but to renew the nation’s governing compact on democratic foundations. The Constitution should serve the people, not bind them to institutional arrangements that no longer work. A new convention is not an abandonment of constitutionalism. It is an effort to rescue constitutional government from obsolescence.

This creates a chief executive who can govern without a mandate from the people, fueling polarization and alienation. The archaic mechanism, originally a concession to slave-holding states to bolster their political power, serves no purpose in a modern democracy other than to disenfranchise urban voters. A rewritten Constitution must institute the direct election of the president, ensuring that the leader of the free world actually reflects the choice of the majority of the free people.

Beyond representation, the Constitution is uniquely negligent in its silence regarding the corruption of modern governance. Perhaps the most damning failure of the current system is its rigidity. The amendment process, requiring a two-thirds majority in Congress and three-quarters of state legislatures, is virtually impossible to achieve in a polarized nation. Rights that are widely accepted by the populace—such as the right to privacy, the right to a clean environment, or the right to vote (which is bizarrely missing a explicit affirmative guarantee)—remain vulnerable because the amendment process is a dead letter. Critics of a new Convention often invoke the specter of chaos, warning that opening the Constitution could lead to the destruction of the Bill of Rights. Introduction: Stop Patching the Unpatchable
Americans treat the Constitution the way a desperate homeowner treats a collapsing roof: every four years we climb up with a bucket of tar and slap on another patch—an amendment here, a Supreme Court dodge there—while the rafters rot underneath. The patches have failed. The rafters are dust. The house is uninhabitable.

  1. The Constitution Was Born Broken
    a. Slavery and the Three-Fifths Bargain. The Founders baked human bondage into the apportionment rules, giving the slavocracy fifty extra House seats and seventy years of veto power over national policy. The “original intent” we are told to revere was to protect property in man.

d. Amendment-by-scripture. The only surviving amendment that curtailed rather than expanded elite privilege was the Twenty-Fourth (poll-tax abolition) in 1964. The formula is designed to fail.

  1. Performance Collapse Since 2000
    a. Minority rule is now the norm. Republicans have lost the popular presidential vote in seven of eight contests, yet appointed six of nine Supreme Court justices. The Senate “majority” that confirmed those judges represented 20 million fewer citizens than the “minority.”

c. The electoral-college map now gives either party a plausible path to the White House with as little as 45 percent of the vote, incentivizing extremist campaigns that mine 40-percent-plus resentment rather than build national consensus.

d. Climate emergencies, pandemics, and AI disruption demand swift, expert coordination. The Constitution instead fragments authority across fifty separate insurance regulators, fifty separate Secretaries of State, and fifty separate National Guards that can be hijacked for culture-war theatrics.

  1. Legitimacy Death Spiral
    Citizens under 35 grow up in a country where:
    • Guns have more rights than schoolchildren, because a geriatric Senate refused even to allow debate on universal background checks supported by 90 percent of the public.
    • The Presidential candidate they overwhelmingly supported can be defeated by 77,000 votes spread across three states.
    • The Court can erase reproductive autonomy overnight, quoting a 1650s English jurist who sentenced women to death for witchcraft.

The natural conclusion is that the rulebook itself is a hustle. When structural reform is impossible inside the rulebook, the incentive is to go outside it—January 6 was a fascist rehearsal, not an aberration.

  1. The Amendment Mirage
    “Why not just pass the amendments you want?” Because the very skew you want to fix (Senate malapportionment, Electoral College, life-tenured judges) is codified inside the amendment rule. Asking the beneficiaries of a rigged game to vote to unrig it is like asking the house to rewrite blackjack so the players always win. Mathematically, under current state populations, a coalition of the twenty-one smallest states can block any amendment even though they contain barely 11 percent of Americans. The threshold is impossibility, not high bar.

  2. The Article V Convention—Safest Explosive Device in the Arsenal
    The Framers, terrified of “excess democracy,” inserted the Convention clause (two-thirds of states apply, Congress must call) as a safety valve they never expected to open. Yet the very act of convening changes the political equilibrium: once 34 states file, Congress loses agenda control; delegates are chosen; the nation spends a year debating first principles instead of Dr. Seuss and gas-stoves. The Convention’s product still needs ratification by three-quarters of the states, so the sky is not the limit—only proposals with massive, trans-partisan support can survive. But the starting gun forces a horizon beyond “What can Manchin tolerate?”

  3. Design Goals for a 2020s Constitution
    a. Equal representation of citizens, not acres. A unicameral or double-majority legislature in which passage requires both a majority of the whole people AND a majority of states—so farmers in Kansas are heard but cannot strangle the majority.

b. A President chosen by the plurality of the national vote, with instant-runoff preferencing to eliminate “spoiler” blackmail.

c. A twelve-year, staggered Supreme Court whose members must retire at the end of the term in which they reach age seventy-five. Confirmation requires a super-majority of the democratic chamber and a minority-party hearing quota, ending strategic silence.

d. A “democracy clause” that automatically voids any state law that disproportionately reduces turnout among racial or age groups, shifting the burden of proof to would-be vote suppressors.

e. Constitutional fast-track: amendments proposed by 60 percent of Congress or two-thirds of states are ratified by a simple national majority in a referendum, provided turnout exceeds 55 percent. No more thirteen-state vetoes.

f. Environmental self-defense: any statute that increases national CO2-equivalent emissions by more than 1 percent over five years must be renewed by a super-majority, reversing the default away from planetary arson.

g. Abolition of felony disenfranchisement and lifetime gun-ownership bans for non-violent ex-prisoners; incarceration must remain under federal standards or forfeit matching funds—no more 50-state race to the bottom.

h. Direct citizen initiative at the federal level: 3 percent of the previous presidential electorate can place a statute on the next ballot, 5 percent can place a constitutional amendment.

i. Right to bodily autonomy (reproductive, gender, end-of-life) grounded in the Equal Protection clause, superseding any 1868 “history-and-tradition” test.

j. Fair representation of territories and the District of Columbia as full voting states or equivalent euro-style “land districts,” ending second-class citizenship for 4 million Americans.

  1. Objections Answered
    “It will run away; they’ll repeal the Bill of Rights.” The ratification gate (thirty-eight states) is identical to the one that today’s minorities already abuse; nothing proposed weakens that check, it only enlarges the agenda space.

“The last Convention threw out the Articles; the next could do worse.” The 1787 Convention had no subsequent ratification requirement; our Convention must still persuade a super-majority of a diverse, media-saturated 50-state polity. That is harder, not easier.

“Better the devil you know.” The devil we know just let a 6-3 Court cripple the EPA, immunize Presidents who send mobs to the Capitol, and green-light open carry in Times Square. Risk aversion is now the riskiest strategy of all.

  1. How to Get There in Ten Years
    Step 1: Build a trans-ideological coalition of large-population states (CA, TX, FL, NY, PA, IL, OH, GA, NC, MI) plus small states whose citizens are tired of being ignored (VT, DE, RI, AK, WY). Step 2: Elect governors and attorneys-general in 2026 on a single promise: “Approve the Convention call on day one; the delegates’ product must be put to a national referendum.” Avoid platform specifics; keep the coalition big enough to trust the people.

Step 3: Run a parallel citizens’ assembly (modeled on Ireland 2012-18) of 150 randomly selected Americans who meet for six months, televised, to draft a baseline charter. This educates the public and pressures delegates not to retrofit the same lobbyist wish-lists.

Step 4: Insist on gender, racial, and age parity among delegates—if the Convention itself looks like 1787, its legitimacy will die in the cradle.

We stand where the French did in 1788, where the Mexicans did in 1916, where the South Africans did in 1990: the ancien régime has exhausted its capacity to reform itself without violence. A Convention is not a picnic; it is a controlled demolition. But controlled is the operative word—the alternative is the uncontrolled demolition already under way: mounting coups, stochastic terrorism, and the slow-motion collapse of a climate that can feed our children.

The 1787 Constitution was never holy scripture; it was a pragmatic hack to get thirteen quarreling debtors to form a customs union. We owe it the same reverence the Romans owed the Twelve Tables—gratitude for the concept, and ruthlessness about its replacement. If Americans cannot muster the nerve to rewrite the rules under which we live, we will soon live under rules written for us by oligarchs, theocrats, and strongmen. Convene the Convention, open the floor, trust a free people to out-perform a slaveholders’ relic. The roof is already on fire; we can either architect a new house or keep praying the smoke doesn’t kill us first.

    B. Fiscal & stewardship package (favorite of conservative COS backers)
    – Balanced-budget amendment with automatic sequester and capital-budget carve-out.
    – Single-subject line-item veto.
    – Term limits for Congress (12 years) and federal judges (24 years).
    – Sunset clause forcing every federal agency, tax break, and regulation to be re-enacted every 10 years.

    C. Rights & governance modernization package
    – Explicit right to vote, overruling Shelby County v. Holder.
    – Privacy/data amendment for the algorithmic era.
    – Equal Rights and reproductive-freedom clauses.
    – Clean anti-corruption language overturning Citizens United; publicly financed campaigns; 7-day disclosure rule.
    – Clear emergency-powers clause: 30-day sunset unless Congress affirms; prohibits deployment of troops against domestic voters.

  4. How a convention could actually improve governance (according to advocates)

    Deliberative mini-public input
    – States could send delegate slates chosen by citizens’ assemblies or sortition panels, forcing the convention to listen to ordinary voters instead of party insiders.

    – Rural states get ECPA-style electronic-property-rights protection; cities get Electoral College reform; fiscal hawks get a long-term budget rule—everyone gets something, so 38-state ratification becomes thinkable.

    Political jolt short of violence
    – Historical pattern (1787, 1933, 1964-65) shows that systemic threats—if visibly addressed—lower extremist recruitment. Supporters say a controlled convention is preferable to the “auto-coup” path taken by other presidential regimes.

    Market credibility bonus
    – A credible exit from perpetual debt-ceiling chicken could lower U.S. borrowing costs by 25–40 bp, saving ≈ $90 billion per year—more than EPA and State-Department budgets combined.

    – States already limit their applications by topic; 28 states have identical “single-subject” COS applications for fiscal and term-limit amendments—only six short of the trigger.

Bottom line
Proponents believe the U.S. has reached the same endpoint the Founders feared: “the people’s branch obstructed, the executive swelling, the states rent asunder.” An Article V convention, they argue, is the only safety valve designed into the system that does not require Washington’s permission. By bundling popular-democracy fixes, fiscal discipline, and anti-corruption rules into a single ratifiable package, a convention could—without revolution or court-packing—restore majority rule while still protecting minority rights and federal structure. Critics see catastrophic risk; supporters see the last lawful way to renovate the house before the roof caves in.

The Case for a New Constitutional Convention

The Constitution Was Built for a Different Country

The Constitution of 1787 was a remarkable political achievement for its time, but it was designed for a small, agrarian republic of fewer than four million people, many of whom were excluded from political life entirely. It was written before political parties became central to governance, before universal suffrage, before industrial capitalism, before modern media, before global military power, before administrative government, before nuclear weapons, before digital surveillance, and before the United States became a continent-spanning, multiracial democracy of more than 330 million people.

This produces a dangerous contradiction: the country needs structural reform, but the ordinary path to reform is nearly impossible.

That is why the Article V convention mechanism exists. It is not an unconstitutional rebellion against the founding charter; it is part of the founding charter. The framers themselves recognized that Congress might become an obstacle to necessary reform. They provided a second route: the states may demand a convention. Using that mechanism would not be a rejection of constitutionalism. It would be constitutionalism in action.

The Senate Is a Democratic Disaster

Perhaps the clearest example of structural failure is the United States Senate. Every state receives two senators regardless of population. As a result, Wyoming, with fewer than 600,000 people, has the same Senate power as California, with nearly 40 million. This is not a minor imperfection. It is a massive distortion of democratic representation.

The Senate gives disproportionate power to smaller, often less diverse states. It allows a minority of the national population to block legislation, confirm judges, shape the federal judiciary, approve treaties, and determine the composition of the Supreme Court. When combined with the filibuster, the Senate becomes even more anti-majoritarian, allowing a minority within a minority to prevent national action.

Defenders of the Senate say it protects federalism. But federalism should not mean that citizens in one state have dozens of times more political power than citizens in another. States are not people. The moral basis of democratic government is political equality among citizens, not equal dignity among geographic units. A modern constitution should not allow representation in one of the most powerful legislative chambers in the world to be determined by state boundaries drawn through conquest, compromise, and historical accident.

The Senate cannot be meaningfully fixed through ordinary politics because the very states that benefit from the distortion can block reform. That is a textbook example of why a broader constitutional reckoning is necessary.

The Electoral College Is Indefensible

The Electoral College is another constitutional structure that has outlived any plausible justification. It can award the presidency to the candidate who loses the national popular vote. It distorts campaigns by concentrating attention on a handful of swing states. It renders millions of votes effectively irrelevant in states dominated by one party. It magnifies polarization and undermines the basic democratic principle that the person who receives the most votes should win.

The presidency is the only nationally elected office, yet the Constitution does not provide for a direct national election. Instead, Americans vote through a state-based mechanism originally shaped by compromises over slavery, federalism, and distrust of direct democracy. In the modern era, the Electoral College serves no noble purpose. It does not produce better presidents. It does not protect small states in any consistent way. It does not encourage national campaigning. It does not prevent demagoguery. It merely creates the possibility that the highest office in the country will be filled against the preference of the electorate.

A government that repeatedly permits minority rule cannot claim to be fully democratic. A new constitution should abolish the Electoral College and establish direct popular election of the president, preferably with ranked-choice voting or a runoff system to ensure majority legitimacy.

The Supreme Court Has Become Too Powerful and Too Unaccountable

The Constitution also fails to provide adequate democratic control over the judiciary. Supreme Court justices serve for life. They are appointed through a politicized process shaped by the Senate’s anti-majoritarian structure and the accidents of timing. A president who loses the popular vote can appoint justices confirmed by senators representing a minority of the population, and those justices can then shape national law for decades.

This is not a healthy constitutional arrangement. Judicial review may be necessary to protect rights and maintain constitutional boundaries, but lifetime rule by nine unelected officials is not democratic. The Court has repeatedly made sweeping decisions on voting rights, campaign finance, reproductive freedom, labor power, executive authority, environmental regulation, and civil rights. Whether one agrees or disagrees with particular decisions, the structural problem remains: enormous political power is concentrated in an institution with weak accountability and life tenure.

A new constitutional order should impose term limits on Supreme Court justices, regularize appointments, clarify the scope of judicial review, and create stronger democratic mechanisms for constitutional interpretation. Constitutional meaning should not depend so heavily on the health, age, and retirement decisions of individual justices.

The Presidency Has Become Dangerously Imperial

The framers feared monarchy, yet the modern presidency has accumulated powers that would have alarmed many of them. Presidents now command a global military, oversee a vast administrative state, direct foreign policy, influence economic policy, issue executive orders, conduct military operations without formal declarations of war, and dominate national political attention.

Congress has repeatedly surrendered authority to the executive, especially in matters of war and emergency power. The result is an imperial presidency: too powerful when occupied by the reckless, too constrained by partisan deadlock when action is needed, and too dependent on informal norms that can be shattered by a determined occupant.

The Constitution does not adequately define or limit modern executive power. It does not provide sufficient mechanisms for emergency governance, war authorization, executive accountability, or removal of officials who abuse public trust. Impeachment has proven too partisan and too blunt to serve as a reliable safeguard. A new constitution should reconsider the presidency itself—perhaps moving toward a parliamentary or semi-parliamentary system in which executive power is more directly accountable to legislative majorities.

The System Produces Gridlock, Not Deliberation

American constitutional design prizes separated powers, checks and balances, bicameralism, federalism, judicial review, and staggered elections. In theory, these mechanisms prevent tyranny. In practice, they often prevent governance.

The modern United States faces urgent problems: climate change, housing shortages, health care costs, technological disruption, immigration reform, inequality, infrastructure decay, gun violence, fiscal instability, and democratic backsliding. Yet the constitutional system makes coherent national action extraordinarily difficult. A party can win the presidency and the House, receive millions more votes for the Senate, and still be unable to pass its agenda. Voters then cannot clearly assign responsibility for success or failure because power is fragmented across institutions.

This is not deliberative democracy. It is veto-point paralysis. A system with too many choke points empowers obstructionists, lobbyists, courts, and minority factions. It rewards performative politics over governing. It encourages parties to campaign on promises they know the structure may prevent them from keeping.

A functioning democracy should allow electoral majorities to govern, subject to clear rights protections and regular elections. If the public dislikes the results, it can vote the governing coalition out. The American system too often denies majorities the ability to act while also denying voters a clear line of accountability.

Federalism Has Become Incoherent and Unequal

Federalism can encourage local experimentation and protect regional diversity. But American federalism often produces inequality of rights and services based on geography. A citizen’s access to health care, voting rights, education quality, labor protections, reproductive freedom, criminal justice standards, and environmental safety can vary dramatically depending on state residence.

Some variation is inevitable in a federal system. But the current arrangement goes far beyond healthy local autonomy. It permits states to undermine national democratic norms, restrict ballot access, entrench partisan power through gerrymandering, and create vast disparities in basic rights. Meanwhile, federal power is often expansive in some areas and strangely limited in others, depending less on coherent principle than on judicial doctrine and political struggle.

A new constitution should define federalism for the modern era. It should protect local self-government where appropriate while establishing firm national guarantees for voting rights, civil rights, education, health, environmental protection, and equal citizenship.

The Constitution Does Not Adequately Protect Democracy Itself

One of the most alarming weaknesses of the current Constitution is that it does not sufficiently protect democratic processes. It leaves much election administration to partisan state officials. It does not explicitly guarantee an individual right to vote in clear, affirmative terms. It does not prohibit partisan gerrymandering. It does not provide uniform national standards for ballot access, districting, election certification, or campaign finance.

A democracy should not rely on unwritten norms and patchwork statutes to secure the basic machinery of elections. The Constitution should explicitly guarantee the right to vote, require fair representation, prohibit political manipulation of election rules, and establish independent institutions for election administration and redistricting.

Without such protections, constitutional democracy becomes vulnerable to manipulation from within. The greatest threat to a republic is not always a coup in the streets; it can be the slow legalistic capture of the rules by those willing to use constitutional gaps to entrench minority power.

Rights Need Modernization

The Bill of Rights and later amendments contain essential protections, but they are incomplete for modern life. The Constitution does not clearly protect privacy in the digital age. It does not guarantee equal rights regardless of sex. It does not explicitly protect reproductive autonomy, data privacy, bodily autonomy, or the rights of future generations to a livable environment. It does not guarantee education, health care, housing, or basic economic security.

One may debate which rights belong in a constitution, but the current document reflects an eighteenth- and nineteenth-century rights framework. Modern constitutional democracies often include clearer commitments to human dignity, social rights, gender equality, environmental protection, and democratic participation. The United States should not assume that its rights tradition is complete simply because it is old.

A new convention would allow Americans to ask foundational questions: What rights should every person possess? What obligations does government have to secure meaningful freedom? How should liberty be protected not only from censorship and unlawful searches, but also from domination by poverty, discrimination, surveillance, and concentrated private power?

The Two-Party System Is Entrenched by Constitutional Design

The Constitution does not mention political parties, but its structure has helped entrench a rigid two-party system. Single-member districts, first-past-the-post elections, presidentialism, and the Electoral College make third parties nearly impossible at the national level. Voters are often forced to choose the lesser of two evils. New movements are absorbed, marginalized, or treated as spoilers.

This system intensifies polarization. Because only two parties are viable, each becomes a sprawling coalition of incompatible factions held together by fear of the other side. Negative partisanship replaces civic trust. Primaries empower ideological extremes. General elections become existential struggles.

A new constitution could adopt proportional representation, ranked-choice voting, multi-member districts, or other electoral systems that allow more parties, more accurate representation, and coalition-building after elections rather than permanent binary warfare. If Americans want a healthier politics, they must change the rules that produce the current one.

Reverence Has Become an Obstacle to Self-Government

The deepest problem may be cultural: Americans have been taught to confuse constitutional reverence with patriotism. But no generation has the moral right to bind all future generations to its institutional compromises. Thomas Jefferson argued that the earth belongs to the living, not the dead. Whether or not one accepts his proposed timetable for constitutional revision, the principle is sound. A democratic people must retain the capacity to rethink its fundamental law.

The framers were not gods. They were political actors operating within the limits, prejudices, and conflicts of their time. To treat their handiwork as untouchable is not fidelity to democracy; it is constitutional ancestor worship. The proper way to honor the founding generation is not to freeze their work forever, but to exercise the same authority they exercised: the authority to constitute government through reflection, debate, and consent.

The Risks of a Convention Are Real—but So Are the Risks of Doing Nothing

Opponents of an Article V convention warn that it could become a “runaway convention.” They fear that existing rights could be weakened, that special interests could dominate, or that partisan actors could hijack the process. These concerns are serious. A convention would need transparent rules, democratic delegate selection, public deliberation, and a clear ratification process.

But the possibility of risk cannot justify permanent paralysis. The current system is already producing constitutional crisis. Minority rule, judicial supremacy, electoral dysfunction, legislative gridlock, executive overreach, and democratic distrust are not hypothetical dangers. They are present realities.

Moreover, any proposed changes from a convention would still require ratification. The convention itself would not automatically rewrite the Constitution by decree. The people, through the states and the ratification process, would still have to approve the result. That is a high bar—and appropriately so. But Americans deserve the opportunity to consider a comprehensive alternative.

The argument against a convention often amounts to this: the system is too broken to risk fixing. That is not prudence. It is surrender.

What a New Constitution Should Consider

A new Constitutional Convention should be broad in scope. It should not be limited to symbolic amendments. It should consider fundamental reforms such as:

  • Abolishing the Electoral College and electing the president by national popular vote.
  • Replacing or radically reforming the Senate to reflect democratic equality.
  • Establishing proportional representation or ranked-choice voting.
  • Creating an affirmative constitutional right to vote.
  • Banning partisan gerrymandering.
  • Establishing independent election administration.
  • Imposing term limits on Supreme Court justices.
  • Clarifying and limiting executive emergency and war powers.
  • Strengthening congressional oversight.
  • Modernizing the Bill of Rights for privacy, equality, bodily autonomy, and digital life.
  • Guaranteeing equal rights regardless of sex, race, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability.
  • Reconsidering the balance between federal and state power.
  • Creating clearer anti-corruption rules and campaign finance standards.
  • Making constitutional amendment easier while still requiring broad democratic support.
  • Considering parliamentary or semi-parliamentary alternatives to presidentialism.

The goal should not be chaos. The goal should be democratic renewal.

Conclusion: A Free People Must Be Able to Reconstitute Their Government

The United States is trapped in a constitutional order that too often frustrates majority rule, empowers minority vetoes, distorts representation, blocks necessary action, and relies on institutions designed for a vastly different world. The problem is not merely bad politicians or polarization or civic ignorance. Those are symptoms. The deeper problem is structural.

A constitution should help a people govern themselves. It should translate public will into accountable action while protecting fundamental rights. It should distribute power fairly. It should be adaptable enough to survive change. The current Constitution increasingly fails these tests.

Calling a new Constitutional Convention under Article V would be bold, disruptive, and risky. But American democracy was born from bold constitutional imagination. The country does not need another round of worshipful nostalgia. It needs the courage to ask whether its basic law still serves its people—and the courage to build something better if it does not.

The Constitution begins with “We the People.” Those words do not belong only to the dead. They belong to the living. If the people are sovereign, then the people must have the right, and at moments of crisis the duty, to rethink the foundations of their government. That moment has arrived.
