Supporters of calling a new United States constitutional convention under Article V argue that the current constitutional system is no longer capable of solving major national problems and that ordinary politics cannot fix the system because the people who benefit from it control the reform process.

Article V provides two ways to propose constitutional amendments: by a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress, or by a convention called when two-thirds of state legislatures — currently 34 states — apply for one. Any proposed amendments would still have to be ratified by three-fourths of the states — currently 38 states — before becoming part of the Constitution.

Supporters see an Article V convention as a way to bypass Congress and force structural reforms.

1. Belief that the federal government has grown beyond constitutional limits

One of the most common arguments is that the federal government has become far more powerful than the framers intended. Supporters often point to the expansion of federal authority through:

  • Broad interpretations of the Commerce Clause;
  • Large federal spending programs;
  • Federal mandates imposed on states;
  • Executive orders and administrative regulations;
  • National agencies exercising quasi-legislative power.

From this perspective, Congress, the presidency, and the federal bureaucracy have accumulated too much authority at the expense of states, local governments, and individuals.

A convention, supporters argue, could restore a better balance of power by proposing amendments that limit federal jurisdiction, restrict regulatory authority, or return more power to the states.

2. Concern over national debt and federal spending

Many advocates believe Congress has proven unable or unwilling to restrain federal spending. They argue that elected officials have strong incentives to promise benefits, borrow money, and avoid politically painful fiscal choices.

A convention could propose amendments such as:

  • A balanced-budget requirement;
  • Limits on federal taxation;
  • Caps on federal spending as a percentage of GDP;
  • Restrictions on unfunded mandates;
  • Supermajority requirements for new taxes or debt increases.

Supporters believe these changes could force long-term fiscal discipline and prevent future generations from being burdened by unsustainable debt.

3. Frustration with congressional gridlock and career politicians

Another major argument is that Congress has become dysfunctional, polarized, and dominated by career politicians who are more focused on reelection than governance.

Supporters often favor amendments imposing:

  • Term limits for members of Congress;
  • Restrictions on congressional pensions or privileges;
  • Limits on lobbying by former members;
  • Ethics reforms;
  • Rules requiring Congress to live under the laws it passes.

They argue that term limits and anti-corruption rules would make elected officials more accountable, reduce the influence of entrenched political networks, and encourage citizen-legislators rather than permanent political careers.

4. Desire to curb the administrative state

Some supporters argue that much of modern law is effectively made by unelected federal agencies rather than by Congress. They believe this weakens democratic accountability because agency officials can issue regulations with major economic and social effects without direct voter control.

A convention could propose amendments requiring:

  • Congressional approval of major regulations;
  • Clearer limits on agency power;
  • Stronger separation-of-powers protections;
  • Easier judicial review of federal rules;
  • Prohibitions on agencies interpreting their own authority too broadly.

Supporters believe this would make government more accountable and restore lawmaking power to elected representatives.

5. Belief that the current Constitution is outdated in some areas

Some advocates, especially those who favor a broader overhaul rather than limited amendments, argue that the Constitution was designed for an 18th-century republic and has not kept pace with modern realities.

They may point to issues such as:

  • The Electoral College;
  • The structure of the Senate;
  • Lifetime tenure for Supreme Court justices;
  • The difficulty of amending the Constitution;
  • Ambiguities over executive power;
  • Modern campaign finance;
  • Digital privacy and surveillance;
  • Emergency powers;
  • War powers;
  • Voting rights and election administration.

From this view, the Constitution has endured for a long time, but some of its mechanisms may no longer serve a large, diverse, technologically advanced modern democracy.

6. Reforming the presidency and executive power

Some supporters believe the presidency has become too powerful regardless of which party controls it. They argue that presidents increasingly govern through executive orders, emergency declarations, military actions, and agency directives.

Possible convention proposals could include:

  • Limits on emergency powers;
  • Stronger congressional control over war powers;
  • Limits on executive orders;
  • Clear rules for presidential immunity and accountability;
  • Changes to impeachment or removal procedures;
  • Reform of pardon powers.

Supporters believe this could reduce the risk of executive overreach and strengthen checks and balances.

7. Reforming the Supreme Court and judiciary

Some advocates believe the federal judiciary has become too powerful or too politicized. They argue that major national questions are often decided by courts rather than by elected bodies.

A convention could propose changes such as:

  • Term limits for Supreme Court justices;
  • A mandatory retirement age;
  • Supermajority requirements for striking down laws;
  • Clearer rules for judicial review;
  • Changes to the appointment and confirmation process;
  • Ethics rules for federal judges.

Supporters believe such reforms could reduce ideological battles over court appointments and make the judiciary more accountable.

8. Election and representation reforms

Some supporters of a constitutional overhaul believe American democracy suffers from distorted representation, partisan gerrymandering, campaign-finance problems, low voter confidence, and inconsistent election rules.

Possible reforms could include:

  • Independent redistricting commissions;
  • National standards for voting access;
  • Campaign finance restrictions or disclosure requirements;
  • Ranked-choice voting or other electoral systems;
  • Clarification of voting rights;
  • Reform or abolition of the Electoral College;
  • Changes to how Senate representation works.

Supporters argue these reforms could make government more representative, reduce polarization, and increase public trust.

9. Breaking the power of entrenched interests

A central argument for a convention is that Congress is unlikely to propose amendments that reduce its own power. Supporters say lawmakers, lobbyists, federal agencies, and political parties all benefit from the current system and therefore have little incentive to change it.

An Article V convention is seen as a mechanism for the states and the people to force reforms from outside Washington, D.C.

In this sense, supporters often describe it as a constitutional “reset button” or a way to restore popular sovereignty.

10. Renewing civic unity and legitimacy

Some supporters believe the United States suffers from a crisis of legitimacy: many citizens no longer trust Congress, the courts, the presidency, the media, or federal institutions. They argue that a national constitutional debate could help the country reconsider its basic principles and rebuild consent around a renewed governing framework.

A convention could, in theory, allow Americans to debate questions such as:

  • What powers should the federal government have?
  • What rights should be expressly protected?
  • How should elections be conducted?
  • What limits should exist on debt, war, taxation, and surveillance?
  • How should power be divided between states and Washington?

Supporters believe this process could modernize the constitutional order and give citizens a greater sense of ownership over their government.

11. Possible benefits supporters claim

Advocates believe a convention could improve governance by producing reforms that ordinary legislation cannot achieve. The supposed benefits include:

  • Greater fiscal responsibility;
  • Reduced federal overreach;
  • Stronger state authority;
  • More accountable elected officials;
  • Less corruption and lobbying influence;
  • Clearer limits on presidential and agency power;
  • A more representative electoral system;
  • Reduced judicial politicization;
  • Stronger protection of individual rights;
  • Better checks and balances;
  • Increased public trust in government.

In short, supporters see an Article V convention as a way to repair what they view as deep structural problems, not merely change policies.

12. Limited convention versus full constitutional replacement

Not all supporters want the same thing. Some advocate a limited convention focused on a few amendments, such as a balanced-budget amendment, term limits, or limits on federal power.

Others favor a broader constitutional convention that could substantially revise or even replace the existing Constitution. These advocates tend to believe that the current system is too broken for piecemeal amendments and that the country needs a more comprehensive redesign.

The difference is important: many people who support an Article V convention for specific amendments do not necessarily support replacing the Constitution entirely.

Summary

Supporters of a new constitutional convention argue that the existing system has produced excessive federal power, unsustainable debt, entrenched political elites, bureaucratic rule, judicial politicization, executive overreach, and public distrust. They believe Congress cannot be trusted to reform itself, so the states must use Article V to propose structural changes.

They see a convention as a way to restore accountability, limit government, modernize outdated institutions, rebalance federalism, and renew the legitimacy of American self-government.

The Case for a New Constitutional Convention: Time for Fundamental Reform

The United States Constitution, ratified in 1788, has served as the foundational legal document for a nation of thirteen agrarian colonies that has since become a continental superpower of 330 million people. While reverence for this document runs deep in American political culture, it is time to confront an uncomfortable truth: the current constitutional framework is failing to meet the challenges of modern governance, and the amendment process has proven too cumbersome to fix it. A new constitutional convention under Article V deserves serious consideration.

The Argument for Radical Reform

Structural Dysfunction Has Become Chronic

The federal government's persistent gridlock is not merely a matter of political will—it is baked into constitutional design. The separation of powers, originally intended to prevent tyranny, now regularly produces paralysis. Government shutdowns, debt ceiling crises, and legislative gridlock recur with predictable regularity because the system allows narrow minorities to block action indefinitely. The Senate's filibuster, combined with the chamber's malapportionment, means that senators representing a small fraction of the population can block legislation supported by the vast majority of Americans.

Representation Has Become Deeply Distorted

The Electoral College and Senate apportionment create a system where voters in Wyoming have roughly 70 times the electoral influence of voters in California. Two presidents in the last six elections have won the presidency while losing the popular vote. This is not democratic legitimacy—it is a structural anomaly that a supermajority of Americans consistently oppose in polling, yet cannot fix because the amendment process itself requires the assent of the very small states that benefit from this distortion.

The Amendment Process Is Effectively Dead

Article V requires two-thirds of both congressional chambers and three-fourths of state legislatures to ratify amendments—a bar so high that only 27 amendments have passed in 235 years, and none addressing structural governance issues since 1971. In an era of intense polarization, achieving this consensus through the traditional congressional route is essentially impossible. A convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures offers an alternate path explicitly provided by the Framers themselves, who anticipated that future generations might need to fundamentally reconsider their arrangements.

The Document Cannot Address Modern Realities

The Constitution was written before industrialization, mass communication, nuclear weapons, climate change, and a globalized economy. Its framers could not have anticipated presidential power over standing armies and nuclear arsenals, the rise of an administrative state necessary to regulate complex modern industries, or the speed at which information and misinformation now travels. We are attempting to govern a 21st-century society with an 18th-century operating system, and patch-work amendments have proven insufficient to the task.

Judicial Supremacy Has Warped Constitutional Meaning

Because formal amendment is so difficult, constitutional change has increasingly occurred through judicial interpretation rather than democratic deliberation. This has transformed the Supreme Court into a quasi-legislative body, with enormous consequences for abortion, campaign finance, voting rights, and executive power determined by unelected judges parsing ambiguous 18th-century text rather than through the deliberate constitutional processes democratic theory would demand.

Answering the Objections

Critics warn that a convention could "run away," producing chaos or a document that strips away hard-won rights. This concern deserves serious weight, but it is not a reason to forswear the process entirely—rather, it argues for careful convention rules, transparent proceedings, and robust ratification requirements (which would remain in place) as safeguards. Every constitutional convention in history has carried risks; the 1787 convention itself exceeded its mandate to merely "amend" the Articles of Confederation. Yet the result, whatever its flaws, was superior to paralysis under the Articles.

The idea of calling a new U.S. Constitutional Convention under Article V—to either overhaul or "replace" the Constitution—is a highly controversial and fringe proposal with no mainstream political or legal support for a full replacement. Crucially, Article V does not authorize a constitutional convention to "replace" the Constitution; it only permits conventions to propose specific amendments, which must then be ratified by 3/4 of states. The term "replace" is misleading—no serious proposal seeks to nullify the entire Constitution. Instead, proponents of a convention typically advocate for targeted amendments (e.g., on fiscal issues, term limits, or campaign finance), but they frequently exaggerate the process as a "reset" for America's governance. Below is a balanced analysis of why some supporters argue for it, the risks involved, and why experts overwhelmingly reject it as dangerous and impractical.

Why Supporters Advocate for an Article V Convention

Supporters (primarily far-right groups like the "Convention of States" project, libertarian-leaning academics, and some Tea Party activists) cite these stated reasons:

  1. Congressional Gridlock and Partisan Deadlock

    • Argument: The existing amendment process requires 2/3 of both House and Senate to propose amendments, which is nearly impossible in today's hyperpartisan Congress. A convention bypasses Congress entirely, allowing states to initiate changes directly.
    • Example: Efforts to pass a balanced budget amendment or term limits for Congress have repeatedly failed in Congress but could theoretically move forward via a convention.

  2. Structural Flaws in the Current System

    • Supporters believe specific issues require systemic fixes that can't be solved by piecemeal amendments:
      • Electoral College: Critics argue it distorts presidential elections (e.g., 2016, 2000) and disincentivizes candidates from campaigning in non-swing states.
      • Senate Representation: Equal state representation (2 senators per state) gives small states disproportionate power (e.g., Wyoming has 0.18% of the U.S. population but 2% of Senate seats).
      • Campaign Finance: The Citizens United decision (2010) allowing unlimited corporate spending in elections is seen as corrupting democracy. A convention could potentially pass an amendment overturning it.
      • House Apportionment: The 1929 law fixed House seats at 435, causing massive district inequality (e.g., Montana's single district has over 1 million people; Rhode Island's two districts average ~530,000 each).
      • Federal Overreach/State Sovereignty: Some states (e.g., Texas) argue the federal government has overstepped its bounds; a convention could clarify federal/state powers.

  3. "Reset" for Democracy

    • A minority of proponents (e.g., certain libertarian or progressive activists) claim the Constitution is "obsolete" due to modern issues like technology, climate change, or economic inequality. They argue a convention could create a more responsive, modern framework—though they rarely specify how.

Why Supporters Believe It Could Improve Governance

They claim a convention could:

  • Bypass Gridlock: States, not Congress, would drive change on contentious issues like school funding, environmental regulations, or social policy.
  • Address Systemic Issues Holistically: Instead of scattered amendments, a convention could reform multiple interconnected problems (e.g., combining electoral college reform with campaign finance rules).
  • Restore "Popular Sovereignty": By involving state legislatures directly, it would return power to "the people" via their state representatives.

Why the Proposal Is Widely Rejected as Dangerous and Impractical

Despite these arguments, almost all legal scholars, historians, and political scientists oppose an Article V convention. Major risks include:

1. "Runaway Convention" Risk: Total Constitutional Collapse

  • The Core Problem: Article V is intentionally vague. There are no rules defining:
    • How delegates are chosen (elected? appointed by state legislatures?).
    • What topics are debated (a "balanced budget" convention could easily shift to repealing civil rights amendments).
    • Standards for ratification (4/5 of states? Or supermajorities for specific sections?).
  • Historical Precedent: The 1787 Constitutional Convention was called to amend the Articles of Confederation but wrote an entirely new Constitution in secret. This is the "runaway convention" nightmare: once convened, delegates could draft a new constitution with no obligation to follow the original mandate.
  • Real-World Danger: If a convention proposed abolishing the Bill of Rights, ending judicial review, or dismantling federalism, ratification would be nearly impossible—but the attempt alone could trigger chaos, consent for amendment could be misinterpreted (e.g., requiring 3/4 state legislatures vs. state conventions), and opponents would have no legal recourse.

2. The Convention Would Embolden Demagogues and Special Interests

  • State-Level Influence: 34 states must formally apply for a convention. Today, interest groups (e.g., conservative Christian groups, corporate lobbyists) could pressure state legislatures to apply for specific amendments, then manipulate delegates.
  • Lack of Transparency: Delegates wouldn't be accountable to voters. A convention could shut out public input, leading to secret deals (unlike Congress, which has hearings, debates, and media scrutiny).

3. It Ignores the Existing Amendment Process

  • 17 Amendments Adopted Since 1789: The existing process has worked for issues like abolishing slavery (13th), granting women's suffrage (19th), and limiting presidential terms (22nd).
  • Recent Successes: The 27th Amendment (congressional pay raises) was ratified in 1992—over 200 years after its proposal—proving the process can handle long delays.
  • Better Alternatives: Incremental reforms via Congress (e.g., campaign finance bills, districting reforms), or state-level actions (e.g., the National Popular Vote compact for president), are safer and more effective.

4. No Practical Path to Success

  • Not Enough States: Only 28 states have active applications for a balanced budget amendment convention. A "general overhaul" convention would require 34 states—and it's unlikely any can agree on a single issue. Many states have rescinded past applications (e.g., Florida, Arizona).
  • Legal Chaos: If a convention is called, Congress would set rules—but states could sue to challenge the process, leading to years of litigation. The Supreme Court has never ruled on an Article V convention, creating untested constitutional ground.

5. The "Replace" Misconception

  • Article V explicitly allows only amendments. To "replace" the Constitution would require a revolutionary act—not a constitutional process. Any attempt to do so would be illegal under the current framework and likely meet armed resistance from federal authorities.

Expert Consensus: An Article V Convention Is a Terrible Idea

  • American Bar Association: Calls for a convention "undesirable" due to "risks of a runaway convention" and "lack of procedures."
  • Harvard Law School Professors: Describe it as a "dangerous policy experiment" that could "dismantle the Bill of Rights."
  • Politicians Across Parties: Even vocal critics of Congress (e.g., Sen. Bernie Sanders) reject a convention. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer stated, "An Article V convention is a terrible idea."
  • Historians: Historian Gordon Wood called it "paper-thin" and "guaranteed to produce a disaster."

Conclusion: The Real Solution Lies Elsewhere

Article V’s amendment pathway—two‑thirds of both chambers of Congress or two‑thirds of state legislatures to propose, and three‑fourths of states to ratify—was deliberately made arduous to protect stability. Even widely supported reforms—such as eliminating the Electoral College, instituting national popular vote, or imposing term limits on Congress—are effectively impossible under the current process. The amendment mechanism, designed for a slower, more deliberative age, now guarantees that the Constitution will remain frozen while the country’s problems accelerate.

The Case for Constitutional Reinvention: Why America Needs an Article V Convention

Introduction

The United States Constitution, ratified in 1788, stands as the world's oldest active written national constitution. Americans often cite this longevity as evidence of the document's genius. But longevity is not inherently virtuous in governance—it can equally signal institutional paralysis, the triumph of procedural obstacles over democratic will, and the entrenchment of arrangements that no longer serve the public good. The time has come for Americans to exercise the power explicitly reserved to them in Article V: to convene a constitutional convention and fundamentally reimagine the framework of self-governance.

This is not radicalism. It is fidelity to the revolutionary premise upon which the nation was founded—that each generation possesses the inherent right to determine the structures under which it lives.

The Founders Expected Constitutional Evolution

The framers themselves harbored no illusions about constitutional permanence. Thomas Jefferson famously argued that constitutions should expire every nineteen years, writing to James Madison that "the earth belongs to the living" and that binding future generations to the dead hand of the past constituted a form of tyranny. Madison, though more cautious, acknowledged the necessity of periodic revision.

Article V itself embodies this expectation. The inclusion of a convention mechanism—bypassing Congress entirely if two-thirds of state legislatures demand it—reveals the framers' recognition that the federal government might one day become too ossified or self-interested to reform itself. They provided the people with a tool for revolutionary restructuring within the constitutional order.

That Americans have never utilized this tool for comprehensive reform represents not wisdom but failure—a collective inability to muster the political will to address systemic dysfunction.

The Amendment Process Has Functionally Failed

Consider the structural impossibility of amendment under current conditions. Article V requires proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress or two-thirds of state legislatures, followed by ratification by three-fourths of states. In contemporary America, where political polarization has reached historic levels and thirteen states representing approximately four percent of the population can block any amendment, this threshold is effectively insurmountable for any significant reform.

The Constitution has been amended only seventeen times since the Bill of Rights—an average of once every fourteen years—and not substantively since 1971. Meanwhile, seismic shifts have transformed American society: industrialization, the rise of the administrative state, the information revolution, globalization, climate change, the emergence of a surveillance-capable security apparatus, and the concentration of unprecedented wealth and corporate power. The Constitution remains silent on all of it, leaving the Supreme Court to retrofit eighteenth-century language to twenty-first-century realities through increasingly strained interpretive gymnastics.

A document that cannot adapt is not stable; it is brittle.

Structural Deficiencies Demand Structural Solutions

The Constitution's failures are not merely procedural but substantive. Consider the accumulation of democratic deficits:

The Senate represents the most malapportioned legislative body in any Western democracy. Wyoming's 580,000 residents enjoy equal representation with California's 39 million—a ratio of roughly 68:1. This arrangement, defensible perhaps in 1787 as a compromise to secure ratification, now produces systematic minority rule. Combined with the filibuster (itself a constitutional accident), the Senate allows senators representing less than twenty percent of the population to obstruct any legislation.

The Electoral College has twice in the past six elections delivered the presidency to the candidate who lost the popular vote. It distorts campaign incentives toward a handful of swing states, renders most Americans' votes symbolically meaningless, and creates persistent legitimacy crises. No other advanced democracy employs such a system.

Presidential power has metastasized far beyond constitutional text. The executive now wages wars without congressional declaration, governs through executive orders that function as legislation, and claims authorities—from emergency powers to executive privilege—that appear nowhere in Article II. The Constitution provides no adequate mechanism for checking a president determined to push constitutional boundaries.

Judicial supremacy, established through Marbury v. Madison rather than constitutional text, has transformed the Supreme Court into an unelected super-legislature. Lifetime appointments, combined with increasingly partisan confirmation processes, have made the Court's composition a matter of actuarial luck rather than democratic deliberation. Constitutional meaning now shifts not through amendment but through the strategic retirement timing of elderly judges.

The absence of positive rights distinguishes the American Constitution from virtually every constitution written since World War II. Rights to education, healthcare, housing, a clean environment, or basic economic security—recognized in the constitutions of Germany, South Africa, and dozens of other democracies—find no home in American fundamental law. The negative liberty framework, innovative in 1787, now appears impoverished against the backdrop of comparative constitutionalism.

Comparative Evidence Supports Constitutional Renewal

The American veneration of constitutional permanence represents not universal wisdom but national peculiarity. The average lifespan of national constitutions is approximately seventeen years. Most mature democracies have rewritten their constitutions within living memory—France in 1958, Germany in 1949, Japan in 1947, South Africa in 1996, and numerous others.

These nations have not descended into chaos. Democratic Germany operates under its fourth constitutional order and remains among the world's most stable democracies. The process of constitutional replacement, far from undermining democratic governance, can reinvigorate it by forcing fundamental conversations about shared values and institutional design.

Americans are not uniquely incapable of deliberating over first principles. The presumption that a convention would inevitably produce chaos reveals more about contemporary cynicism than historical necessity.

The Legitimacy Deficit

Beneath structural concerns lies a deeper problem of democratic legitimacy. The Constitution was drafted by approximately fifty-five white male property owners, many of them slaveholders, deliberately insulated from popular pressure. Women, Black Americans, Indigenous peoples, and property-less white men had no voice in its creation. The ratification process excluded the vast majority of the adult population.

We honor this document, amended but fundamentally unchanged in structure, as the supreme law binding 330 million people in circumstances its authors could not have imagined. The normative claim that past generations—particularly past generations from whom most living Americans descend in neither blood nor ideology—may permanently constrain the self-governing choices of the present demands justification it increasingly cannot supply.

Constitutional legitimacy in a democracy must rest on more than historical inheritance. It requires ongoing consent—what the philosopher Jürgen Habermas calls the "constitutional patriotism" that emerges when citizens recognize fundamental law as genuinely their own. A convention would provide an opportunity not merely to fix structural defects but to relegitimize constitutional government through contemporary democratic participation.

Addressing the Objections

Critics will raise several objections, each demanding serious response:

"A convention would be hijacked by extremists." This concern assumes that contemporary Americans, given deliberative opportunity, would make worse choices than eighteenth-century slaveholders. It also ignores available procedural safeguards: delegate selection through democratic election, transparency requirements, supermajority ratification thresholds, and the precedent of state constitutional conventions that routinely produce moderate, workable documents.

"The results would be unpredictable." Unpredictability is not inherently undesirable; it is the nature of genuine political deliberation. The current system produces predictable dysfunction—is that preferable? Moreover, ratification by three-fourths of states provides a check against genuinely extreme outcomes.

"The Constitution has served us well." This assessment survives scrutiny only if one ignores the Civil War, the century of Jim Crow that followed, the democratic deficits enumerated above, and the contemporary governance paralysis that leaves pressing problems—climate change, healthcare, inequality, infrastructure decay—perpetually unaddressed. The Constitution has coincided with American prosperity; causation is another matter.

"We should pursue ordinary politics first." This objection assumes that ordinary politics can solve structural problems that ordinary politics systematically produces. Gerrymandering, campaign finance corruption, and counter-majoritarian institutions create self-reinforcing pathologies that resist reform from within. Structural problems require structural solutions.

A Convention as Democratic Renewal

Imagine a convention that seriously deliberated over questions Americans have not confronted collectively since 1787:

Should we remain one nation or constitute ourselves as a looser federation? How should representation be apportioned—by population, by region, by interest? What rights should be guaranteed against both governmental and private power? How should judicial review operate, if at all? What checks should constrain executive power in an age of nuclear weapons and instant communication? How should subnational units relate to national power? What obligations do citizens and government owe one another?

These questions have been answered provisionally by historical circumstance. A convention would allow contemporary Americans to answer them deliberately.

The process itself would hold value independent of outcome. Forcing the nation into fundamental deliberation about constitutional design could reinvigorate civic engagement, clarify areas of genuine consensus and legitimate disagreement, and provide democratic education at scale. Even failed proposals would establish baselines for future reform.

Conclusion

The American Constitution represents an extraordinary achievement of political philosophy applied to statecraft. But honoring the framers' accomplishment does not require embalming their choices as permanent. The revolutionary generation would have been appalled by descendants who treated their pragmatic compromises as sacred text beyond revision.

Article V provides the mechanism. The question is whether this generation of Americans possesses the imagination, the courage, and the democratic faith to use it.

The evidence of systemic dysfunction surrounds us: a government increasingly incapable of addressing collective problems, democratic processes captured by concentrated wealth, polarization amplified by institutional design, and a growing sense among citizens across the political spectrum that the system serves those within it rather than the public at large.

We need not accept this condition as permanent. The Constitution can be rewritten because the framers knew it would need to be. The only remaining obstacle is the belief that what is must forever be—a belief incompatible with the American experiment at its most basic level.

A new constitutional convention would be neither betrayal nor revolution. It would be the fulfillment of a promise made in 1787 and waiting ever since to be honored: that the people retain the ultimate authority to reconstitute the terms of their own governance.

It is time.

A Call to Constitutional Renewal

Fellow Americans,

Two hundred and thirty-seven years ago, extraordinary men gathered in Philadelphia and did something revolutionary—not with muskets, but with ideas. They looked at a failing system, the Articles of Confederation, and they did not tinker at the margins. They did not patch. They reimagined.

And they gave us a gift: Article V. A mechanism for we the people to do exactly what they did—to gather, to deliberate, and to remake our governing charter when the old one no longer serves.

That time has come again.

I. The System Is Broken—And Everyone Knows It

Look around you. What do you see?

A Congress paralyzed by partisan warfare, where legislation dies not on merit but on procedural manipulation. A Senate where a single senator can hold hostage the appointments of an entire government. A Supreme Court whose composition has become a blood sport, where lifetime appointments turn nine unelected lawyers into the most powerful policymakers in the nation.

We have a presidency that has accumulated powers the Founders never imagined and would never have sanctioned. Executive orders that function as legislation. Emergency powers that never end. Wars fought for decades without congressional declaration.

We have an Electoral College that has twice in twenty years handed the presidency to the candidate who lost the popular vote—not because the system worked, but because the system is an artifact of compromises made to accommodate slavery.

We have a Senate where Wyoming's 580,000 citizens have the same voice as California's 39 million. Where the filibuster—a procedural accident never mentioned in the Constitution—allows a minority to rule as tyrants over the majority.

We have a House of Representatives gerrymandered into absurdity, where politicians choose their voters rather than voters choosing their politicians. Where "safe seats" breed extremism because the only election that matters is the primary.

And underlying all of this? A campaign finance system that has transformed our democracy into an auction house, where policy goes to the highest bidder and ordinary citizens are spectators to their own governance.

Tell me: Is this what Madison envisioned? Is this what Hamilton defended? Is this Jefferson's dream?

No. It is a perversion of their vision, calcified by time, corrupted by power, and desperately in need of renewal.

II. The Founders Expected Us to Do This

We are not betraying the Founders by convening. We are honoring them.

Thomas Jefferson wrote that each generation should have its own constitution—that "the earth belongs to the living, not the dead." He suggested constitutions should expire every nineteen years, forcing each generation to actively choose its government rather than inherit it passively.

We have waited more than twelve Jeffersonian generations. We have amended the Constitution only seventeen times since the Bill of Rights—and most of those amendments corrected obvious moral failures like slavery and the exclusion of women from voting.

The Founders were not prophets. They were brilliant, yes—but they were also men of their time, architects of compromise, some of them enslavers, none of them able to foresee the internet, nuclear weapons, multinational corporations, climate change, or a nation of 330 million people stretching across a continent and beyond.

They gave us Article V precisely because they knew their work was imperfect. George Mason refused to sign the Constitution in part because he feared the amendment process was too difficult. He was right. It has proven nearly impossible to amend through Congress—because Congress will never vote to limit its own power.

But there is another path. Article V allows two-thirds of state legislatures to call a convention. This is the path the Founders left for us when the federal government becomes too entrenched, too self-interested, too deaf to the people's voice.

This is not revolution. This is constitutional renewal through constitutional means.

III. What Must Change

Let me be specific, because this is not about abstract grievances. This is about building something better.

We need a democracy that actually represents the people.

  • Abolish or reform the Electoral College so that every vote counts equally, regardless of geography.
  • End partisan gerrymandering through independent redistricting commissions mandated by the Constitution itself.
  • Consider proportional representation so that the full spectrum of American political thought has voice.

We need a Congress that can actually govern.

  • Eliminate or reform the filibuster at the constitutional level.
  • Create a more balanced Senate—perhaps through weighted voting or expanded membership.
  • Mandate transparent, recorded votes on all substantive matters.

We need a judiciary accountable to the living.

  • Establish term limits for Supreme Court justices—eighteen years, staggered, so each president appoints two per term.
  • Depoliticize confirmation through supermajority requirements or nonpartisan nominating commissions.
  • Clarify the scope of judicial review so unelected judges cannot substitute their policy preferences for democratic choice.

We need an executive branch restored to its proper bounds.

  • Constrain emergency powers with mandatory sunset provisions and congressional reauthorization.
  • Require congressional approval for military action beyond immediate defense.
  • Limit executive orders to genuine execution of law, not lawmaking by decree.

We need money out of politics.

  • Overturn Citizens United not through a Court's change of heart, but through the sovereign voice of the people.
  • Establish public financing of elections as a constitutional principle.
  • Declare that corporations are not persons and money is not speech.

We need rights updated for our time.

  • Enshrine the right to vote as fundamental, protected against state suppression.
  • Consider rights to privacy, to a healthy environment, to education.
  • Clarify the Second Amendment in ways that honor both tradition and public safety.

These are not radical ideas. Every one of them has been proposed by serious scholars, endorsed by millions of citizens, blocked only by the very dysfunction they seek to remedy.

IV. To the Skeptics

I hear the objections. Let me answer them.

"A convention would be hijacked by extremists."

Look at our current government and tell me we haven't already been hijacked. A convention is transparent. Delegates must be chosen, proposals must be debated, and any amendments must still be ratified by three-fourths of states. The guardrails are real.

"We might lose rights we have."

Thirty-eight states would have to ratify any change. Thirteen states can block anything. Do you truly believe three-fourths of America would abolish free speech? Abandon religious liberty? This fear is not respect for the Constitution—it is paralysis dressed as prudence.

"The process is dangerous and unpredictable."

What we have now is dangerous. What we have now is a slow-motion collapse of democratic legitimacy. The danger is not change—it is stagnation. It is a sclerotic system lurching from crisis to crisis, unable to solve problems everyone knows must be solved.

"Let's use the regular amendment process."

We have tried. For decades. Congress will not propose amendments that limit congressional power. The courts will not restrain themselves. The states are our only path—the path the Founders explicitly provided.

V. This Is Our Moment

Throughout history, great nations have faced moments of decision. Moments when the old ways no longer serve, when the choice is renewal or decline.

Rome faced such moments and chose emperors over republics.

Britain faced such moments and chose gradual reform, preserving liberty.

America has faced such moments before. In 1787, we chose boldly. In 1865, we chose painfully. In 1920 and 1964 and 1971, we chose to expand the circle of democracy.

Now it is our turn.

We are not combatants seeking to impose one vision on another. We are citizens seeking common ground. Left and right, urban and rural, old and young—we all know the system is failing. We disagree on solutions, yes. But that is what a convention is for: deliberation, debate, compromise, creation.

The Founders argued bitterly. They nearly failed many times. But they kept talking. They kept listening. And they built something that has endured for centuries.

We can do this again. We must do this again.

VI. The Call

So I call upon every state legislature: Exercise your Article V power. Join the movement for a convention.

I call upon every citizen: Demand this of your representatives. Make constitutional renewal a voting issue. Organize, agitate, educate.

I call upon scholars and lawyers: Draft model amendments. Imagine better structures. Prepare the intellectual groundwork.

I call upon the young: This is your future. The Constitution you inherit will shape your children's lives and your grandchildren's possibilities. Do not accept a broken inheritance. Demand better.

And I call upon the skeptics: Engage. Bring your concerns into the process. Help design the rules. Your caution is valuable—channel it into safeguards, not obstruction.

Conclusion

We hold these truths to be self-evident: that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that when any form of government becomes destructive of the ends of liberty and justice, it is the right of the people to alter or abolish it.

We need not abolish. We must alter.

The tool is in our hands. Article V is not a relic—it is an invitation. An invitation left for us by founders who trusted that Americans would always have the courage to improve upon their work.

Let us prove worthy of that trust.

Let us gather.

Let us debate.

Let us build.

Not a second America, but a better America. An America whose government finally reflects the values we profess. An America where every voice counts, every vote matters, and every citizen stands equal before the law.

The convention is not the end of the American experiment. It is the continuation of it.

The Founders began a project. Let us be the generation that perfects it.

Thank you.

Model Response:

The Case for a Second Constitutional Convention: Why America Must Remake Its Founding Document

Introduction

The United States Constitution is among the most admired governing documents in human history. It has endured for over two centuries, survived civil war, industrialization, and global conflict, and provided a framework that generations of Americans have genuinely cherished. Acknowledging all of this is necessary before making the argument that follows: the Constitution, in its current form, has become a serious obstacle to legitimate self-governance, and the problems it creates are now severe enough that Americans should seriously consider convening an Article V constitutional convention to fundamentally restructure the American system of government.

This is not an argument made lightly, nor one driven by partisan frustration with particular election outcomes. It is an argument grounded in structural analysis — the observation that several foundational features of the American constitutional order produce systematic distortions of democratic representation, create dangerous governance failures, and have proven effectively impossible to fix through ordinary constitutional amendment. The document's designers, brilliant as they were, could not anticipate a nation of 335 million people, a permanently professionalized federal government, a two-party duopoly, the administrative state, or the technological conditions of modern democracy. The resulting mismatch between the Constitution's architecture and contemporary governing needs is not a minor maintenance problem. It is a foundational crisis.

The Amendment Process Has Failed

The most important preliminary argument is deceptively simple: the existing amendment process cannot fix the Constitution's structural problems, which means that a convention is the only realistic path to meaningful reform.

Article V requires a proposed amendment to pass both chambers of Congress by a two-thirds supermajority and then be ratified by three-fourths of state legislatures. This process has produced only 27 amendments in 235 years, 10 of which were ratified almost immediately as the Bill of Rights. The last structural amendment — the 26th, lowering the voting age — was ratified in 1971. For over fifty years, no structural change to the American governing framework has occurred.

This is not because the Constitution is perfect. It is because the amendment process is so extraordinarily difficult that it requires a near-consensus that almost never exists in a divided nation. Worse, the process is deliberately resistant to changes that would affect the distribution of power among the very actors who must approve amendments — Congress and state legislatures. Asking Congress to amend away its own dysfunction, or asking small states to ratify amendments that would reduce their structural advantages, is asking turkeys to vote for Thanksgiving. The ordinary amendment process, for structural questions, is simply not a viable mechanism.

This creates a profound democratic problem. When a governing framework contains serious flaws that cannot be corrected through normal institutional channels, the document effectively becomes self-entrenching against the will of the governed. The Founders themselves recognized this. Jefferson famously argued that constitutions should be rewritten every generation, specifically to prevent the dead from governing the living. Madison designed the Article V convention process precisely as a safety valve — a mechanism by which the people could bypass a dysfunctional Congress to fundamentally revise the governing framework. The convention option has never been used. It is past time to use it.

The Senate Is Indefensible

Of all the structural problems in the American constitutional order, the United States Senate is the most serious and the most difficult to justify on democratic grounds.

The Constitution gives each state two senators regardless of population. This was a political compromise at the founding — the so-called Great Compromise — not a principled statement about representation. It was necessary to convince small states to ratify the Constitution. Madison himself considered it a serious flaw, arguing in Federalist No. 62 that it could only be justified by the "peculiar situation" requiring compromise, not by any principle of justice or good government.

The practical consequences today are staggering. Wyoming has roughly 580,000 residents and two senators. California has nearly 40 million residents and two senators. This means a Wyoming voter has approximately 68 times more representation in the Senate than a California voter. The Senate does not merely tilt representation toward small states — it creates a system in which a majority of Americans can be systematically outvoted by a minority on virtually every major question of national policy.

This distortion has grown dramatically more consequential over time. When the Constitution was written, the population ratio between the largest and smallest states was roughly 13 to 1. Today it exceeds 70 to 1 and continues to grow as population concentrates in urban states. The geographic sorting of American politics — in which the Republican coalition is heavily concentrated in less populous states and the Democratic coalition is concentrated in more populous ones — means that Senate malapportionment now produces persistent, systematic partisan distortion, not merely occasional aberrations.

The Senate's supermajority requirement for overcoming filibusters compounds this problem severely. Legislation supported by senators representing 70 percent of the American population can be blocked by senators representing 30 percent. This is not a feature of republican government — it is a feature of oligarchic veto power. The consequence is legislative paralysis on virtually every significant policy question, from healthcare to climate to immigration, not because Americans lack majority preferences on these issues, but because the Senate's structure prevents those majority preferences from being enacted.

No serious democratic theory justifies this arrangement. Federalism — the genuine value of allowing states to govern themselves — does not require that the federal government be systematically biased toward less populous states. Federal systems around the world, from Germany to Australia to Canada, manage robust state autonomy without giving citizens of smaller jurisdictions dramatically more influence over national policy than citizens of larger ones. America's Senate malapportionment is not federalism. It is a historical accident that has become a democratic pathology.

The Electoral College Is an Anti-Democratic Relic

The Electoral College was designed for a world that no longer exists. It presupposed that ordinary citizens lacked sufficient information to choose a president directly, that partisan political parties did not exist, and that electors would exercise genuine independent judgment. None of these conditions obtain today. The Electoral College now functions as a mechanism for distorting presidential elections in ways that contradict the democratic principle that every vote should count equally.

The consequences are familiar but worth stating precisely. Five presidents have taken office after losing the national popular vote: John Quincy Adams, Rutherford Hayes, Benjamin Harrison, George W. Bush, and Donald Trump. In a country of 335 million people governed by a single executive with enormous power over war, peace, regulatory policy, and judicial appointments, it is simply indefensible that the candidate preferred by fewer Americans repeatedly wins the presidency.

Beyond the inversion problem, the Electoral College creates a system in which presidential campaigns focus almost entirely on a handful of competitive "swing states" while treating the vast majority of Americans — those living in safely Republican Texas or safely Democratic California — as politically irrelevant. A voter in Pennsylvania or Wisconsin matters enormously to a presidential campaign. A voter in Oklahoma or New York matters almost not at all. This is not a minor electoral quirk. It means that presidential policy is systematically shaped to serve the interests of swing-state constituencies at the expense of majorities of Americans whose votes are effectively predetermined.

The standard defenses of the Electoral College are weaker than their proponents acknowledge. The argument that it protects small states is somewhat overstated — in practice, large competitive states like Pennsylvania and Michigan receive more campaign attention than small safe states. The argument that it preserves federalism conflates the mechanism of state-based tallying with the principle of state autonomy, which would survive a popular vote. The argument that it produces decisive outcomes is empirically contested and, in any case, seems like a poor justification for overriding democratic majorities. A constitutional convention should seriously consider replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote or a ranked-choice system that preserves majority preference.

The Supreme Court Has Become Ungovernable

The Supreme Court's structure — nine justices, appointed for life, confirmed by a Senate with its own anti-majoritarian distortions, exercising unreviewable power over constitutional interpretation — has produced a governance crisis that worsens with each passing decade.

The problem is not judicial review itself, which serves crucial functions in protecting rights and checking legislative excess. The problem is the combination of lifetime tenure, small court size, and a confirmation process that has become a high-stakes political war of total consequence. Because every vacancy is enormously consequential and permanent, nominations have become the most intense battlefield in American political life, producing systematic distortion of both judicial selection and Senate politics.

The consequences are severe. Justices now routinely serve into their eighties and beyond, creating random variation in court composition based entirely on the accident of when justices die or retire relative to presidential terms. Mitch McConnell's refusal to hold hearings on Merrick Garland's nomination, followed by the confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett days before a presidential election, illustrated how completely the process has been captured by raw political calculation. The resulting court, perceived by significant portions of the public as illegitimately constituted, has issued sweeping decisions on abortion, gun rights, administrative power, and election law that a substantial majority of Americans oppose. The gap between the Court's direction and public preferences is a democratic crisis, not merely a policy disagreement.

A constitutional convention should consider reforms that most democratic theorists have found compelling: term limits for justices (perhaps 18 years, staggered so that each presidential term produces two appointments), expanded court size, supermajority requirements for striking down federal legislation, or some combination thereof. These reforms require constitutional amendment. The ordinary amendment process cannot produce them because the institutional actors who would need to approve them benefit from the current arrangement. Only a convention has a realistic path to achieving them.

The Structural Bias Toward Minority Rule

Taken together, the Senate, the Electoral College, and the Supreme Court constitute a systematic bias in the American constitutional order toward minority rule. This is not a partisan observation — it is a structural one that would concern any democratic theorist examining the system from first principles.

Consider the cumulative effect: A president can take office having received fewer votes than his opponent (Electoral College). That president's party can control the Senate while representing fewer Americans than the opposing party (Senate malapportionment). That majority can confirm Supreme Court justices who then strike down legislation supported by large majorities (life tenure on a small court). This chain of minority-to-majority power transmission is not an occasional malfunction. It is, increasingly, the normal operation of the American constitutional system.

The consequences for governance are severe. Policies supported by substantial majorities of Americans — background checks for firearm purchases, higher minimum wages, pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants who arrived as children, drug pricing negotiation for Medicare — repeatedly fail to become law or are struck down by courts, not because they lack majority support, but because the constitutional structure allows minority vetoes at multiple points. When governing institutions systematically fail to translate majority preferences into policy, the result is eroded public trust, political alienation, and the kind of democratic frustration that historically produces anti-democratic responses.

This is the most important argument for a constitutional convention: the current system does not merely fail to produce good policy. It produces a form of governance that cannot, in its current form, claim democratic legitimacy in any meaningful sense. A government that systematically overrepresents rural voters, that allows presidents to take office without popular majorities, that permits a small group of unelected judges with life tenure to nullify majority will — this is not self-government. It is an aristocratic system wearing democratic clothes.

The Founders' Intent Supports Reform

Opponents of a constitutional convention frequently invoke the Founders as guardians of the existing order. This gets the Founders almost exactly backward.

The men who wrote the Constitution were radicals by the standards of their time. They had just completed a revolution against existing authority and were engaged in an act of founding that explicitly repudiated the legal framework (the Articles of Confederation) under which they were supposed to be operating. The Constitutional Convention of 1787 was itself an unauthorized act — delegates were sent to amend the Articles, not to replace them entirely. The Founders were, in practice, precisely the kind of bold constitutional reformers whose memory is now invoked to block constitutional reform.

More importantly, the Founders explicitly provided for the possibility of fundamental revision. Jefferson's view that constitutions should expire every generation is well known. Less appreciated is that Madison — the primary architect of the Constitution — included the convention option in Article V specifically because he understood that governing documents require fundamental revision as circumstances change. The convention mechanism was not a minor procedural afterthought. It was a recognition that no generation could anticipate all future needs and that the people must retain the ultimate authority to remake their governing framework.

Hamilton, in Federalist No. 85, addressed critics who feared that a constitutional convention would produce chaos. His argument was that the amendment process — including the convention option — reflected confidence in the people's capacity for self-governance. To argue today that Americans cannot be trusted to revise their own governing framework is to adopt a position far more paternalistic and distrustful of democracy than anything the Founders contemplated.

Addressing the Objections

Several serious objections to a constitutional convention deserve honest engagement.

The "runaway convention" concern holds that a convention, once convened, could not be limited to specific topics and might produce radical changes that most Americans would not want. This is a genuine concern with genuine historical support — the 1787 Convention itself exceeded its mandate. However, there are important responses. First, any constitution produced by a convention would still require ratification by three-fourths of states, meaning that truly radical departures from American values could not be imposed. Second, the concern about a runaway convention must be weighed against the acknowledged cost of not holding one — namely, a constitutional order that systematically fails to produce democratic governance. The choice is not between a risky convention and a stable status quo. It is between a risky convention and a slowly failing constitutional system.

The concern about bad actors holds that a constitutional convention could be captured by well-funded interest groups, extremist factions, or bad-faith political actors who would use it to entrench rather than correct anti-democratic features. This concern is serious. It suggests not that a convention should never be held, but that it should be held under carefully designed rules for delegate selection, transparency, and deliberation. It also suggests timing matters — a convention convened under conditions of extreme partisan polarization might produce a worse outcome than one convened under conditions of relative democratic stability. These are arguments for careful design, not categorical opposition.

The incrementalist objection holds that the problems identified here, while real, should be addressed through ordinary political processes rather than fundamental constitutional revision. This was a reasonable position in 1990. It is less reasonable after thirty years in which gridlock, structural dysfunction, and the anti-majoritarian features of the system have worsened rather than improved. The incrementalist case requires showing a realistic path to reform through existing mechanisms. Given that the Senate will not voluntarily reduce its own power, that small states will not voluntarily reduce their structural advantages, and that the amendment process requires supermajorities that cannot be assembled on structural questions, that path does not currently exist.

What a New Constitution Should Achieve

A constitutional convention should not approach its work as mere renovation. It should approach it as an opportunity to design, from reasonably principled first principles, a governing framework adequate to twenty-first century American democracy. Several structural changes deserve serious consideration:

Democratic representation: Replace Senate equal-state representation with a system that better reflects population while preserving meaningful state-level representation — perhaps a reformed Senate with proportional elements, or a unicameral legislature with robust minority protections. Abolish or fundamentally reform the Electoral College in favor of a national popular vote or ranked-choice system.

Judicial reform: Establish term limits for Supreme Court justices, create a regularized nomination process, expand the court to reduce the consequences of individual vacancies, and consider supermajority requirements for striking down democratically enacted legislation.

Electoral integrity: Enshrine the right to vote affirmatively in the Constitution (currently absent), establish independent redistricting as a constitutional requirement, and consider proportional representation provisions to reduce the pathologies of two-party duopoly.

Separation of powers modernization: Clarify the war powers balance between Congress and the executive, establish meaningful oversight mechanisms for the administrative state, and address the concentration of executive power that has grown dramatically since the Constitution was written.

Updated rights framework: Incorporate rights that have been recognized by democratic consensus but lack constitutional foundation — privacy, healthcare access, environmental protection — while preserving and strengthening the Bill of Rights.

Conclusion

The argument for a second constitutional convention is, ultimately, an argument for taking democracy seriously. It is an argument that self-governance is not merely a historical inheritance to be administered and defended, but an ongoing project that requires the courage to confront structural failures honestly.

The current American constitutional order has serious, well-documented, and increasingly severe structural problems that prevent it from translating majority preferences into governance. The ordinary amendment process cannot fix these problems. The institutions that would need to approve such fixes benefit from the current arrangement. The result is a system that increasingly fails its own democratic premises.

The Founders were not afraid of fundamental constitutional revision. They undertook it themselves, without authorization, because they understood that governing documents must serve the living and not the dead. The Article V convention mechanism exists precisely for this moment — not to destroy the American constitutional tradition, but to fulfill its deepest aspiration: government of the people, by the people, and for the people.

That aspiration is worth fighting for. A constitutional convention, designed carefully and held in good faith, is the most promising mechanism currently available for realizing it.

  • Two-thirds of both congressional houses, or two-thirds of state legislatures calling a convention
  • Three-fourths of states (38) to ratify

  • Small minorities can permanently block changes with broad popular support

Separation of powers gridlock

The administrative state problem

  • This contradicts separation of powers doctrine but courts have largely permitted it

  • Supporters argue career politicians become unresponsive to constituents and captured by special interests

  • Clarify Commerce Clause limits

  • No living American consented to be governed by this document
  • Democratic legitimacy requires periodic renewal of foundational arrangements
  • Other democracies regularly revise constitutions - France is on its Fifth Republic
  • Treating the Constitution as quasi-sacred prevents honest assessment of whether it serves current needs

Thomas Jefferson famously suggested constitutions should expire every 19 years, roughly one generation. This argument holds that the founders themselves did not intend permanent entrenchment.

Specific Groups and Their Motivations

Convention of States Project (conservative/libertarian)

  • Focused on fiscal restraint, term limits, limiting federal power
  • Claims applications from roughly 19 states

These are legitimate intellectual and political arguments, not fringe positions.

Whether they justify the significant risks and uncertainty of a convention is a separate question requiring honest assessment of what a convention might actually produce given current political conditions, who would control it, and whether the ratification threshold provides adequate protection against radical change most Americans would not support.
